stem:
The equations of three planes $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ are

$$2x + 5y - z = 3$$
$$3x + y + 5z = -2$$
$$5x + \alpha y + 4z = \beta$$

respectively, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants. When $\alpha = -3$ and $\beta = 1$, find the coordinates of the point where all the 3 planes meet. $[1]$

The planes $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ intersect in a line $l$.

parts.text: Find a vector equation of $l$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
(Stem) With $\alpha = -3$, $\beta = 1$ the three equations are $2x+5y-z = 3$, $3x+y+5z = -2$ and $5x-3y+4z = 1$. Solving simultaneously gives $x = 1$, $y = 0$, $z = -1$ (check: $2+0+1=3$; $3+0-5=-2$; $5-0-4=1$). The three planes meet at $(1,\ 0,\ -1)$.

(i) The direction of $l$ is perpendicular to both normals:

$\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 26 \\ -13 \\ -13 \end{pmatrix} = -13\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Taking $z = 0$ in $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$: $2x + 5y = 3$ and $3x + y = -2$ give $x = -1$, $y = 1$, so $(-1,\ 1,\ 0)$ lies on $l$.

$l: \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.

parts.text: Show that the shortest distance from the point $(1,\ 3,\ 2)$ to $l$ is $2\sqrt{3}$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Let $A = (-1,\ 1,\ 0)$ on $l$ and $P = (1,\ 3,\ 2)$, so $\overrightarrow{AP} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

Shortest distance $= \dfrac{\left|\overrightarrow{AP} \times \mathbf{d}\right|}{|\mathbf{d}|}$ with $\mathbf{d} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2(1)-2(1) \\ 2(-2)-2(1) \\ 2(1)-2(-2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -6 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$

Shortest distance $= \dfrac{\sqrt{0 + 36 + 36}}{\sqrt{4+1+1}} = \dfrac{6\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{3}} = 2\sqrt{3}$ (shown).

parts.text: Given that all 3 planes meet in the line $l$, find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
If all three planes meet in $l$, then $l$ lies in $p_{3}$.

The direction of $l$ must be perpendicular to the normal of $p_{3}$:

$\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ \alpha \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = -10 + \alpha + 4 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = 6$

The point $(-1,\ 1,\ 0)$ must satisfy $p_{3}$: $5(-1) + 6(1) + 4(0) = \beta \Rightarrow \beta = 1$.

$\alpha = 6$, $\beta = 1$.

parts.text: Given instead that the three planes have no point in common, what can be said about the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$?
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
If $\alpha \neq 6$, the normal of $p_{3}$ is not perpendicular to the direction of $l$, so $l$ meets $p_{3}$ at a point and the three planes DO have a common point.

Hence for no common point we need $\alpha = 6$, so that $p_{3}$ is parallel to $l$, together with $\beta \neq 1$, so that $l$ does not lie in $p_{3}$.

$\alpha = 6$ and $\beta \neq 1$.

parts.text: If the planes $p_{1}$ and $p_{4}$ are parallel and the point $(1,\ 3,\ 2)$ is equidistant from these two planes, find the equation of the plane $p_{4}$ in scalar product form.
parts.label: v
parts.solution:
Since $p_{4}$ is parallel to $p_{1}$, it has the same normal, so $p_{4}: \mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = d$.

For the point $(1,\ 3,\ 2)$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 2 + 15 - 2 = 15$.

Distance to $p_{1}$: $\dfrac{|15 - 3|}{\sqrt{30}} = \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{30}}$. Distance to $p_{4}$: $\dfrac{|15 - d|}{\sqrt{30}}$.

Equidistant $\Rightarrow |15 - d| = 12 \Rightarrow d = 3$ or $d = 27$. Since $d = 3$ gives $p_{1}$ itself, $d = 27$.

$p_{4}: \mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 27$.

stem: Answer the following.

parts.text:
A curve $C$ is defined by the equation $xy + y^{2} - x^{3} = 7$.

Find the coordinates of the point where the tangent line to the curve $C$ is parallel to the $y$-axis and state the equation of this tangent line.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Differentiating $xy + y^{2} - x^{3} = 7$ implicitly with respect to $x$:

$y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 3x^{2} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3x^{2} - y}{x + 2y}$

The tangent is parallel to the $y$-axis when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is undefined, i.e. $x + 2y = 0$, so $x = -2y$.

Substituting into the curve: $(-2y)y + y^{2} - (-2y)^{3} = 7$

$-2y^{2} + y^{2} + 8y^{3} = 7 \Rightarrow 8y^{3} - y^{2} - 7 = 0$

$y = 1$ is a root, so $(y-1)\left(8y^{2} + 7y + 7\right) = 0$. The quadratic has discriminant $49 - 224 < 0$, so $y = 1$ is the only real root.

Then $x = -2(1) = -2$, giving the point $(-2,\ 1)$ and tangent line $x = -2$.

parts.text:
A curve is defined parametrically by the equations $x = at$, $y = \dfrac{a}{t^{2}}$. The fixed point $P$ on the curve has parameter $p$.

Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point $P$, leaving your answer in terms of $a$ and $p$. $[3]$

Given that the normal at point $P$ does not meet the curve again, find exactly the range of values of $p$. $[4]$
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\dfrac{2a}{t^{3}}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{2}{t^{3}}$.

At $P$ (where $t = p$) the tangent gradient is $-\dfrac{2}{p^{3}}$, so the normal gradient is $\dfrac{p^{3}}{2}$.

$P$ has coordinates $\left(ap,\ \dfrac{a}{p^{2}}\right)$, so the normal is

$y = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}\left(x - ap\right) + \dfrac{a}{p^{2}}$.

For the normal to meet the curve again, substitute $x = at$, $y = \dfrac{a}{t^{2}}$:

$\dfrac{a}{t^{2}} - \dfrac{a}{p^{2}} = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}\left(at - ap\right)$

$\dfrac{1}{t^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{p^{2}} = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}(t - p)$

$\dfrac{p^{2} - t^{2}}{t^{2}p^{2}} = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}(t-p) \Rightarrow \dfrac{(p-t)(p+t)}{t^{2}p^{2}} = -\dfrac{p^{3}}{2}(p-t)$

Since $t \neq p$ for another intersection, divide by $(p-t)$:

$\dfrac{p+t}{t^{2}p^{2}} = -\dfrac{p^{3}}{2} \Rightarrow 2(p+t) = -p^{5}t^{2} \Rightarrow p^{5}t^{2} + 2t + 2p = 0$

The normal does not meet the curve again when this quadratic in $t$ has no real root:

Discriminant $= 4 - 4\left(p^{5}\right)(2p) < 0 \Rightarrow 4 - 8p^{6} < 0 \Rightarrow p^{6} > \dfrac{1}{2}$

$|p| > \dfrac{1}{2^{1/6}}$, i.e. $p < -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[6]{2}}$ or $p > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt[6]{2}}$.

stem: Answer the following.

parts.text: An arithmetic progression, $A$, has first term, $a$, and a non-zero common difference, $d$. The first, fifth and fourteenth term of $A$ are equal to the third, second and first term of a geometric progression $G$ respectively.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Show that the common ratio of $G$ is $\dfrac{4}{9}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
The terms of $A$ are $a$, $a+4d$ and $a+13d$, which are the 3rd, 2nd and 1st terms of $G$.

So $G$ has first term $a+13d$, second term $a+4d$ and third term $a$, giving

$r = \dfrac{a+4d}{a+13d} = \dfrac{a}{a+4d}$

$(a+4d)^{2} = a(a+13d)$

$a^{2} + 8ad + 16d^{2} = a^{2} + 13ad$

$16d^{2} = 5ad$

Since $d \neq 0$, $16d = 5a$, i.e. $a = \dfrac{16d}{5}$.

$r = \dfrac{a}{a+4d} = \dfrac{\frac{16d}{5}}{\frac{16d}{5} + 4d} = \dfrac{\frac{16d}{5}}{\frac{36d}{5}} = \dfrac{16}{36} = \dfrac{4}{9}$ (shown).

subparts.text: Determine the ratio of the sum to infinity of $G$ to the sum to infinity of the odd-numbered terms of $G$.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Let the first term of $G$ be $A_{1}$ and $r = \dfrac{4}{9}$. Since $|r| < 1$ both sums to infinity exist.

Sum to infinity of $G$: $S_{\infty} = \dfrac{A_{1}}{1-r}$.

The odd-numbered terms of $G$ are $A_{1},\ A_{1}r^{2},\ A_{1}r^{4},\ \ldots$ — a geometric progression with first term $A_{1}$ and common ratio $r^{2}$, so their sum to infinity is $\dfrac{A_{1}}{1-r^{2}}$.

Ratio $= \dfrac{A_{1}}{1-r} \div \dfrac{A_{1}}{1-r^{2}} = \dfrac{1-r^{2}}{1-r} = 1 + r = 1 + \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{13}{9}$.

parts.text: In January 2001, John borrowed $\$29\,000$ from a bank. Interest was charged at $4.5\%$ per year and was calculated at the end of each year starting from 2001. John planned to pay back a fixed amount of $\$x$ on the first day of each month, starting from the first month after his graduation. John graduated from his study at the end of 2004 and started payment in January 2005.
parts.label: b

subparts.text:
Show that the amount owed at the end of 2005 was $[1]$

$$1.045^{5}(29000) - 1.045(12x).$$

Taking 2005 as the first year, find an exact expression for the amount John owed at the end of the $n$th year, simplifying your answer in terms of $n$ and $x$. $[3]$
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
From January 2001 to the end of 2004, interest is charged four times with no repayment, so the amount owed at the end of 2004 is $29000\left(1.045\right)^{4}$.

During 2005 John pays $12x$, and interest is charged at the end of the year:

Amount at end of 2005 $= \left[29000(1.045)^{4} - 12x\right](1.045) = 1.045^{5}(29000) - 1.045(12x)$ (shown).

Continuing, each year's $12x$ of repayments earns interest for the remaining years, so at the end of the $n$th year (2005 being the first):

Amount $= 1.045^{n+4}(29000) - 12x\left(1.045 + 1.045^{2} + \cdots + 1.045^{n}\right)$

The bracket is a geometric series with first term $1.045$, ratio $1.045$ and $n$ terms:

$= 12x \cdot \dfrac{1.045\left(1.045^{n} - 1\right)}{1.045 - 1} = 12x \cdot \dfrac{1.045}{0.045}\left(1.045^{n} - 1\right) = \dfrac{836x}{3}\left(1.045^{n} - 1\right)$

Amount owed $= 1.045^{n+4}(29000) - \dfrac{836x}{3}\left(1.045^{n} - 1\right)$.

subparts.text: If the loan must be repaid within 8 years from John's graduation, find the minimum amount, correct to the nearest dollar, John must pay each month.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: $x \geq 418.11$, so the minimum monthly amount is $\$419$
subparts.solution:
The loan is repaid within 8 years when the amount owed at the end of the 8th year is at most zero:

$1.045^{12}(29000) - \dfrac{836x}{3}\left(1.045^{8} - 1\right) \leq 0$

$\dfrac{836x}{3}\left(1.045^{8} - 1\right) \geq 1.045^{12}(29000)$

$1.045^{8} = 1.42210$, $1.045^{12} = 1.69588$, so

$x \geq \dfrac{29000(1.69588)}{\frac{836}{3}(0.42210)} = \dfrac{49180.6}{117.625} = 418.11$

Since payments are whole dollars, the minimum monthly amount is $\$419$.

parts.text:
By using the method of difference, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = k - \mathrm{f}(n)$, where $k$ is a constant and $\mathrm{f}(n)$ is an expression in $n$ to be found. $[4]$

Explain why $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)}$ is a convergent series and state the value of the sum to infinity. $[2]$
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
By partial fractions, $\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = \dfrac{1}{r+2} - \dfrac{1}{r+3}$ (with $A = 1$, $B = -1$).
$\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = \sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{1}{r+2} - \dfrac{1}{r+3}\right)$
Telescoping gives $= \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{n+3}$ (Shown), so $k = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $\mathrm{f}(n) = \dfrac{1}{n+3}$.
As $n \to \infty$, $\dfrac{1}{n+3} \to 0$, so $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} \to \dfrac{1}{3}$. Hence the series is convergent.
$S_\infty = \dfrac{1}{3}$

parts.text: In the sketch of the curve $y = \sqrt{\ln(3+x)}$, $0 \le x \le 5$, the region under the curve is split into 5 vertical strips of equal width of 1 unit.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show by means of a sketch that $\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{4}\sqrt{\ln(3+x)}$ is less than the actual area under the graph.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: The five rectangles using the left endpoint of each strip lie entirely below the increasing curve, so their total area $\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{4}\sqrt{\ln(3+x)}$ is an underestimate of the actual area under the graph. (See sketch.)

subparts.text: Find a similar expression that will give a value more than the actual area under the graph.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: $\displaystyle\sum_{x=1}^{5}\sqrt{\ln(3+x)}$ is more than the actual area under the graph.

subparts.text: Find the value of the actual area under the graph, giving your answer to 3 decimal places.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{5}\sqrt{\ln(3+x)}\,dx = 6.43421 = 6.434\ \text{unit}^2$

subparts.text: Using the expression in part (i), find the absolute percentage error in the estimate.
subparts.label: iv
subparts.solution:
$\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{4}\sqrt{\ln(3+x)} = 6.22772$ (to 5 dp)
Absolute percentage error $= \left|\dfrac{6.43421 - 6.22772}{6.43421}\right| \times 100\% = 3.21\%$

subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
The sequence $1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, \ldots$ has first term 1 and common difference 3.
$T_n = 3n - 2$

subparts.text: Find the $80$th term of the sequence.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Write down the smallest and largest four-digit number of the sequence.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
$T_n = 3n - 2$ gives remainder 1 when divided by 3.
Smallest four-digit term: smallest $T_n \geq 1000 \Rightarrow T_n = 1000$.
Largest four-digit term: largest $T_n \leq 9999 \Rightarrow T_n = 9997$.
Smallest $= 1000$, Largest $= 9997$

subparts.text:
The point $P$ on the Argand diagram represents the complex number $w$ given by $w = u + iv$, where $u$ and $v$ are real and positive.
Explain algebraically why $arg(kw) = arg(w)$ for any real constant $k > 1$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Since $w = u + iv$ with $u > 0$ and $v > 0$:
$kw = ku + ikv$ with $ku > 0$ and $kv > 0$.

$\arg(w) = \tan^{-1}\frac{v}{u}$

$\arg(kw) = \tan^{-1}\frac{kv}{ku} = \tan^{-1}\frac{v}{u} = \arg(w)$

subparts.text:
Points $Q$ and $R$ represent the complex numbers $kw$ and $ikw$, where $k$ is a real constant and $k > 1$.
On the same Argand diagram in the Printed Answer Booklet, plot the points $Q$ and $R$. Show clearly the geometrical relationship between the points $P,Q$ and $R$. [2]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Graph sketch showing $Q$ on the ray $OP$ extended and $R$ obtained by rotating $Q$ by $90°$ anticlockwise about $O$.
subparts.solution:
[See solution diagram: Argand diagram]

$Q$ represents $kw$: on the same ray from $O$ through $P$, but further from $O$ (since $k > 1$).
$R$ represents $ikw$: obtained by rotating $OQ$ by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about $O$.

Geometrical relationship: $OR$ is perpendicular to $OQ$, and $OR = OQ$.

parts.text: In another Argand diagram, the points $A,B$ and $C$ represent the complex numbers $z,f(z)$ and $f(f(z))$ respectively, where $f(z) = z^{2} - 2z$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show that $f(f(z)) - f(z) = z(z - 2)(z - 3)(z + 1)$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text:
It is given that $ABC$ is a right-angled triangle, described in an anticlockwise sense, with a right angle at $B$, and $BC = mBA$, where $m$ is a positive real constant.
By considering $\frac{f(f(z)) - f(z)}{f(z) - z}$, or otherwise, show that [2]
$$\left( z - 2 \right)\left( z + 1 \right) = mi$$
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Rotate $\overrightarrow{BC}$ anticlockwise by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ about $B$ to obtain $m\overrightarrow{BA}$:
$i[f(f(z)) - f(z)] = m(z - f(z))$

$\frac{f(f(z)) - f(z)}{f(z) - z} = -\frac{m}{i} = mi$

Note $f(z) - z = z^2 - 3z = z(z-3)$.

$\frac{z(z-2)(z-3)(z+1)}{z(z-3)} = mi$

$(z-2)(z+1) = mi$ (shown)

subparts.text: In the case where $z = x + 2i$, where $x$ is a positive real number, find $x$ and $m$. Hence obtain the complex number represented by the point $B$.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
$z = x + 2i$ where $x > 0$.

$(z-2)(z+1) = mi$
$z^2 - z - 2 = mi$
$(x+2i)^2 - (x+2i) - 2 = mi$
$x^2 + 4ix - 4 - x - 2i - 2 = mi$
$(x^2 - x - 6) + i(4x - 2) = mi$

Compare real parts: $x^2 - x - 6 = 0$
$(x-3)(x+2) = 0$
$x = 3$ (reject $x = -2$ since $x > 0$)

Compare imaginary parts: $m = 4x - 2 = 4(3) - 2 = 10$

$f(z) = z^2 - 2z = (3+2i)^2 - 2(3+2i)$
$= 9 + 12i - 4 - 6 - 4i$
$= -1 + 8i$

$B$ represents the complex number $-1 + 8i$.

parts.text: The curves $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ have equations $\frac{x^{2}}{9} - \frac{y^{2}}{4} = 1$ and $y^{2} + x^{2} = k^{2}$ respectively, where $k$ is a positive constant.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Sketch $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ on the same diagram, stating the coordinates of any points of intersection with the axes and the equations of any asymptotes.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
[See diagram]
$C_1$: $\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{4} = 1$ is a hyperbola with vertices $(\pm 3, 0)$ and asymptotes $y = \pm\frac{2}{3}x$.
$C_2$: $y^2 + x^2 = k^2$ is a circle centred at origin with radius $k$, intersecting axes at $(\pm k, 0)$ and $(0, \pm k)$.

subparts.text: State the range of values of $k$ for $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ to intersect.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: For $C_1$ and $C_2$ to intersect, $k \geq 3$ (since $k > 0$).

subparts.text: State the equations of the common lines of symmetry for both $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$. [1]
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution: Common lines of symmetry for both $C_1$ and $C_2$ are $x = 0$ and $y = 0$.

parts.text: The distribution of marks obtained by 80 students for Mathematics Test 1 is summarised by a box-and-whisker plot shown below.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Find (a) the median mark, [1] (b) the interquartile range of the marks. [2]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) From the box plot: median $= 42$.
(b) Upper quartile $= 58$; lower quartile $= 31$.
Interquartile range $= 58 - 31 = 27.$

subparts.text: The same group of students sat for Mathematics Test 2. The distribution of marks for Test 2 is summarised in the table below. Make 2 comparisons between the marks for Test 1 and marks for Test 2. Use figures to support your answers.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: (1) Students performed better in Test 2: median 50 > 42. (2) Test 1 marks were more consistent: IQR 27 < 30 (Test 2).
subparts.solution:
1. The students performed better in Math Test 2, as the median mark is 50 (Test 2) compared to 42 (Test 1).
2. The students' marks in Math Test 1 are more consistent, as the interquartile range is 27 marks compared to 30 marks (Test 2: UQ − 25th percentile $= 60 - 30 = 30$).

parts.text: The same group of 80 students sat for Additional Mathematics Test. $\dfrac{1}{10}$ of them failed and a quarter of them scored distinction for the test.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Two students are selected from the class at random. (a) Find the probability that both students passed the test. [2] (b) Find the probability that one student failed the test and the other student passed the test but did not score a distinction. [3]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Total students $= 80$; failed $= \dfrac{1}{10} \times 80 = 8$; passed $= 72$; distinction $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 80 = 20$; passed but no distinction $= 72 - 20 = 52$.
(a) P(both passed) $= \dfrac{72}{80} \times \dfrac{71}{79} = \dfrac{5112}{6320} = \dfrac{639}{790}.$
(b) P(one failed, one passed without distinction) $= 2 \times \dfrac{8}{80} \times \dfrac{52}{79} = \dfrac{2 \times 8 \times 52}{80 \times 79} = \dfrac{832}{6320} = \dfrac{52}{395}.$

subparts.text: A mistake has been discovered when recording the marks of the Additional Mathematics Test. To correct the mistake, 2 marks need to be added to all students' marks. Describe the effect this correction would have on the mean and standard deviation of the marks of this test.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Mean increases by 2 marks; standard deviation remains unchanged
subparts.solution:
Adding a constant $c$ to every data value:
• shifts the mean by $c$ (mean increases by $2$ marks),
• does NOT change the standard deviation (no impact on spread).

A hemispherical bowl of fixed radius $r$ cm is filled with water. Water drains out from a hole at the bottom of the bowl at a constant rate.

Use your graph to show that when the depth of water is $h$ cm (where $h \leq r$), the volume of water in the bowl is given by
$$V = \frac{\pi h^2}{3}(3r - h)$$ [3]
parts.label: i
parts.answer: The graph is the lower half of the circle of centre $(0,\ r)$ and radius $r$, passing through $(-r,\ r)$, $(0,\ 0)$ and $(r,\ r)$. The volume result follows by rotating this arc about the $y$-axis.
parts.solution:
**Sketch.** $x^2 + (y-r)^2 = r^2$ is a circle of centre $(0,\ r)$ and radius $r$. The restriction $y \leq r$ keeps the lower semicircle, which runs from $(-r,\ r)$ down through the origin $(0,\ 0)$ and back up to $(r,\ r)$. This is the cross-section of the bowl, with its lowest point at the origin.

**Volume.** Rotating the arc about the $y$-axis gives the bowl. Water to depth $h$ occupies $0 \leq y \leq h$, and from the equation $x^2 = r^2 - (y - r)^2 = 2ry - y^2$. Hence
$$V = \pi\int_0^h x^2\,dy = \pi\int_0^h \left(2ry - y^2\right)dy = \pi\left[ry^2 - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^h = \pi\left(rh^2 - \frac{h^3}{3}\right)$$
$$V = \frac{\pi h^2}{3}\left(3r - h\right)$$ as required.

parts.text: Given that a full bowl of water would become empty in 24 s, find the rate of decrease, in terms of $r$ and $h$, of the depth of water in the bowl at the instant when the depth of water is $h$ cm.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
When the bowl is full, $h = r$, so
$$V_{\text{full}} = \frac{\pi r^2}{3}(3r - r) = \frac{2\pi r^3}{3}$$

The water drains at a constant rate and the bowl empties in 24 s, so
$$\frac{dV}{dt} = -\frac{1}{24}\cdot\frac{2\pi r^3}{3} = -\frac{\pi r^3}{36}$$

From $V = \pi\left(rh^2 - \frac{h^3}{3}\right)$,
$$\frac{dV}{dh} = \pi\left(2rh - h^2\right)$$

By the chain rule,
$$\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{dV}{dt} \div \frac{dV}{dh} = \frac{-\frac{\pi r^3}{36}}{\pi\left(2rh - h^2\right)} = -\frac{r^3}{36\left(2hr - h^2\right)}$$

The depth is therefore decreasing at a rate of $\dfrac{r^3}{36\left(2hr - h^2\right)}$ cm s$^{-1}$.

parts.text: Without any differentiation, determine, in terms of $r$, the slowest rate at which the depth of water is decreasing.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
The rate of decrease $\dfrac{r^3}{36\left(2hr - h^2\right)}$ is slowest when the denominator, and hence $2hr - h^2$, is greatest.

Completing the square, $2hr - h^2 = r^2 - (h - r)^2$, which is greatest when $h = r$ — the largest depth allowed — giving the value $r^2$. (No differentiation is needed.)

The slowest rate of decrease is therefore
$$\frac{r^3}{36r^2} = \frac{r}{36}\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$$

The planes $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ have equations $\mathbf{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 0$ and $\mathbf{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} = 6$ respectively.

parts.text: Find a vector equation of $l$, the line of intersection between $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
A direction vector of $l$ is perpendicular to both normals:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} (1)(-2) - (-1)(-1) \\ (-1)(2) - (1)(-2) \\ (1)(-1) - (1)(2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 0 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix} = -3\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$
A point on both planes: $(2, -2, 0)$ satisfies $2 - 2 - 0 = 0$ and $4 + 2 - 0 = 6$.
Hence $l: \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix},\ \lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.

parts.text:
Another line, $l_{1}$, has equation $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$, where $\mu$ is a real parameter. Use the result in part (i) to show that $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $l_{1}$ have exactly one common point of intersection. (You are not allowed to use any calculator for this part of the question.) [3]

A third plane, $p_{3}$, has equation $\mathbf{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = d$. If $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ have a common line of intersection, show that $b = -1$. [1]
parts.label: ii
parts.answer: Shown. The unique common point is $(0, -2, -2)$.
parts.solution:
Every point common to $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ lies on $l$, so a common point of $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $l_{1}$ is a point of intersection of $l$ and $l_{1}$.
Equating: $2 + \lambda = 2 + \mu$, $-2 = \mu$, $\lambda = 8 + 5\mu$.
From the second equation $\mu = -2$; the first then gives $\lambda = -2$; the third gives $8 + 5(-2) = -2 = \lambda$, which is consistent.
So there is exactly one solution, $\lambda = \mu = -2$, giving the single common point $(0, -2, -2)$ (shown).

If $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ have a common line of intersection, that line must be $l$, so $l$ lies in $p_{3}$ and the direction of $l$ is perpendicular to the normal of $p_{3}$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 @@ 0 @@ 1 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 @@ a @@ b \end{pmatrix} = 1 + b = 0 \Rightarrow b = -1$ (shown).

parts.text: If it is further given that $p_{2}$ bisects the acute angle between $p_{1}$ and $p_{3}$, find the equation for $p_{3}$ completely, in scalar-product form.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
From part (ii), $\mathbf{n}_{3} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ a \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\mathbf{n}_{1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{n}_{2} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$.
If $p_{2}$ bisects the acute angle between $p_{1}$ and $p_{3}$, then $p_{2}$ makes equal angles with $p_{1}$ and $p_{3}$:
$\frac{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{1}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\right|\left|\mathbf{n}_{1}\right|} = \frac{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{3}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\right|\left|\mathbf{n}_{3}\right|}$
$\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\left|4-a\right|}{\sqrt{2+a^{2}}} \Rightarrow \sqrt{3}\sqrt{2+a^{2}} = \left|4-a\right|$
$3\left(2+a^{2}\right) = (4-a)^{2} = 16 - 8a + a^{2} \Rightarrow 2a^{2} + 8a - 10 = 0 \Rightarrow a^{2} + 4a - 5 = 0$
$(a+5)(a-1) = 0 \Rightarrow a = -5$ or $a = 1$.
$a = 1$ gives $\mathbf{n}_{3} = \mathbf{n}_{1}$, so $p_{3}$ would be parallel to $p_{1}$ and could not form an angle with it; reject $a = 1$.
Hence $\mathbf{n}_{3} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, and since $(2, -2, 0)$ lies on $l \subset p_{3}$,
$d = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 2 + 10 + 0 = 12$
$p_{3}: \mathbf{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 12$

This question is about the roots of polynomial equations in $\mathbb{C}$ and the fifth roots of 32.

parts.text: Consider the equation $az^{3} - 9z^{2} + bz - 5 = 0$, where $a$ and $b$ are real constants.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: One root of the equation $az^{3} - 9z^{2} + bz - 5 = 0$ is $z = 2 - i$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Since $a$ and $b$ are real, the non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs, so $z = 2 + i$ is also a root.
$\left( z - (2 - i) \right)\left( z - (2 + i) \right) = z^{2} - 4z + 5$ is therefore a factor.
The constant term of the cubic is $-5$, so the remaining linear factor must be $az - 1$:
$az^{3} - 9z^{2} + bz - 5 = \left( z^{2} - 4z + 5 \right)(az - 1)$
Expanding: $az^{3} - z^{2} - 4az^{2} + 4z + 5az - 5 = az^{3} - (1 + 4a)z^{2} + (4 + 5a)z - 5$
Comparing $z^{2}$: $-(1 + 4a) = -9 \Rightarrow a = 2$.
Comparing $z$: $b = 4 + 5(2) = 14$.

subparts.text: Hence find all the roots of the equation in part (a)(i) in exact form.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
With $a = 2$ and $b = 14$ the equation is $2z^{3} - 9z^{2} + 14z - 5 = 0$.
As $a$ and $b$ are real and $2 - i$ is a root, its conjugate $2 + i$ is also a root.
A cubic with real coefficients has three roots, so the third root must be real.
From the factorisation $\left( z^{2} - 4z + 5 \right)(2z - 1) = 0$, the third root is $2z - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow z = \frac{1}{2}$.
The roots are $2 - i$, $2 + i$ and $\frac{1}{2}$.
(Check: product of roots $= \frac{5}{2}$, and $(2 - i)(2 + i)\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = 5 \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2}$.)

parts.text:
Solve the equation $w^{5} = 32$, giving the roots in the form $re^{i\alpha}$, where $r > 0$ and $-\pi < \alpha \leq \pi$. [3]
When shown in an Argand diagram, these roots form the vertices of a polygon. Deduce the area of this polygon in the form $k\sin\theta$, where $k$ and $\theta$ are values to be determined. [2]
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$w^{5} = 32 = 32e^{i(2k\pi)}$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$
$w = 32^{\frac{1}{5}}e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{5}} = 2e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{5}}$
Taking $k = -2,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2$ to keep $-\pi < \alpha \leq \pi$:
$w = 2e^{-i\frac{4\pi}{5}},\ 2e^{-i\frac{2\pi}{5}},\ 2,\ 2e^{i\frac{2\pi}{5}},\ 2e^{i\frac{4\pi}{5}}$
The five roots all have modulus 2 and are equally spaced by $\frac{2\pi}{5}$, so they are the vertices of a regular pentagon inscribed in the circle $|w| = 2$.
The pentagon splits into 5 congruent triangles, each with two sides of length 2 and included angle $\frac{2\pi}{5}$:
Area $= 5 \times \frac{1}{2}(2)(2)\sin\frac{2\pi}{5} = 10\sin\frac{2\pi}{5}$
So $k = 10$ and $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{5}$ (area $\approx 9.51$).

parts.text:
Joanne begins a monthly savings plan. In the first month, she puts $\$1000$ into her savings, and for each subsequent month she puts 5% more than in the previous month. How many months would it take for Joanne's total savings to first exceed $\$20000$? [3]

Jim starts a monthly savings plan two months later than Joanne with an initial savings of $\$2000$, and for each subsequent month he puts $\$100$ more than in the previous month. The table below shows the person whose total savings exceeds the other person's total savings in the $N$th month since Joanne started saving.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline N & \text{Person with more total savings in the } N\text{th month} \\ \hline 1 & \text{Joanne} \\ 2 & \text{Joanne} \\ 3 & \text{Joanne} \\ 4 & \text{Joanne} \\ 5 & \text{Jim} \\ 6 & \text{Jim} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ n-1 & \text{Jim} \\ n & \text{Joanne} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \hline \end{array}$

Find the value of $n$. [4]
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Joanne's monthly amounts form a geometric progression with first term $1000$ and common ratio $1.05$.
Total after $n$ months $= \frac{1000\left(1.05^{n}-1\right)}{1.05-1} = 20000\left(1.05^{n}-1\right)$.
$20000\left(1.05^{n}-1\right) > 20000 \Rightarrow 1.05^{n} > 2 \Rightarrow n > \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.05} = 14.20669908$
Since $n$ is a whole number of months, it takes 15 months.

In the $N$th month since Joanne started, Jim has been saving for $N-2$ months, and his amounts form an arithmetic progression with first term $2000$ and common difference $100$.
Jim's total $= \frac{N-2}{2}\left[2(2000) + (N-3)(100)\right] = \frac{N-2}{2}\left[4000 + 100(N-3)\right]$.
Joanne's total $= 20000\left(1.05^{N}-1\right)$.
When $N = 49$: Jim $= \frac{47}{2}(8600) = 202100$ and Joanne $= 20000\left(1.05^{49}-1\right) = 198427$, so Jim has more.
When $N = 50$: Jim $= \frac{48}{2}(8700) = 208800$ and Joanne $= 20000\left(1.05^{50}-1\right) = 209349$, so Joanne has more.
Hence the first month after month 5 in which Joanne again has more is $n = 50$.

parts.text: Suppose instead that Joanne puts a fixed amount of $\$1000$ into her bank account on the first day of every month. The interest rate is $r\%$ per month, so that on the last day of each month the amount in the account on that day is increased by $r\%$. At the end of 2 years, the total amount in her account will be at least $\$30000$. Find the smallest value of $r$, correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: $r \geq 1.74302$, so the least value of $r$ is $1.8$
parts.solution:
Let $k = 1 + \frac{r}{100}$. The deposit made at the start of month 1 earns interest for 24 months, the deposit at the start of month 2 for 23 months, and so on.
Total at the end of 24 months $= 1000k + 1000k^{2} + \cdots + 1000k^{24} = \frac{1000k\left(k^{24}-1\right)}{k-1}$.
$\frac{1000k\left(k^{24}-1\right)}{k-1} \geq 30000 \Rightarrow \frac{k\left(k^{24}-1\right)}{k-1} \geq 30$
Solving with the GC gives $k \geq 1.0174302$, that is $r \geq 1.74302$.
Checking to 1 decimal place: $r = 1.7$ gives a total of $\$29831.6 < \$30000$, while $r = 1.8$ gives $\$30079.6 \geq \$30000$.
Hence the smallest value of $r$ is $1.8$.

parts.text: Which interval contains the median age? [1]
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Interval $30$--$35$.

parts.text: Find the estimated mean age of the members. [1]
parts.label: b
parts.solution: Estimated mean $= \dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f} = \dfrac{6 \times 22.5 + 14 \times 27.5 + 19 \times 32.5 + 11 \times 37.5 + 10 \times 42.5}{60} = \dfrac{1975}{60} = 32.9$ (3 s.f.).

parts.text: Find the estimated standard deviation of the members. [1]
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{\sum f x^2}{\sum f} = \dfrac{6 \times 22.5^2 + 14 \times 27.5^2 + 19 \times 32.5^2 + 11 \times 37.5^2 + 10 \times 42.5^2}{60} = \dfrac{67225}{60}$.
Estimated standard deviation $= \sqrt{\dfrac{67225}{60} - \left(\dfrac{1975}{60}\right)^2} = 6.07533 = 6.08$ (3 s.f.).

parts.text: The members in the club remain unchanged after $5$ years.
parts.label: d

subparts.text: Write down the new mean age of the members. [1]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: New mean age $= 32.9 + 5 = 37.9$.

subparts.text: Without calculating, explain why the standard deviation remains unchanged. [1]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Adding a constant to every data value shifts the mean but does not change the spread, so the standard deviation is unchanged.
subparts.solution: After $5$ years, the age of every member is increased by $5$, and the new mean age is also increased by $5$. Hence $\sum f[(x + 5) - (\bar{x} + 5)]^2 = \sum f(x - \bar{x})^2$ remains unchanged. $\Rightarrow$ SD $= \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum f(x - \bar{x})^2}{60}}$ remains unchanged.

The fruit distribution company employs $15$ workers. One of the $15$ workers is selected at random. The probability that it is a woman working part time is $\dfrac{1}{5}$. Two of the $15$ workers are selected at random. The probability that they are both men working full time is $\dfrac{1}{5}$. Complete the table of information about the $15$ workers in the company.
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|} \hline  & \text{Part-time workers} & \text{Full-time workers} \\ \hline \text{Men} & & \\ \hline \text{Women} & & 4 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Men part-time $= 1$, Men full-time $= 7$, Women part-time $= 3$ (Women full-time $= 4$).
parts.solution:
Number of part-time women workers $= \dfrac{1}{5} \times 15 = 3$
Total number of male workers $= 15 - 7 = 8$
Let the number of part-time male workers be $x$:
$\dfrac{8 - x}{15} \times \dfrac{8 - x - 1}{14} = \dfrac{1}{5}$
$(8 - x)(7 - x) = 42$
$x^2 - 15x + 14 = 0$
$x = 14$ (rejected) or $x = 1$
So: Men part-time $= 1$, Men full-time $= 7$, Women part-time $= 3$, Women full-time $= 4$.

parts.text: Vectors $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are such that $\mathbf{w} \neq \mathbf{0}$ and $4\mathbf{w} \times \mathbf{v} = 3\,\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w}$.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Show that $\mathbf{w} = \lambda(3\mathbf{u} + 4\mathbf{v})$, where $\lambda$ is a constant.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$4\mathbf{w} \times \mathbf{v} = 3\,\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w}$ (Note: $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w} = -\mathbf{w} \times \mathbf{u}$)
$4\mathbf{w} \times \mathbf{v} - 3\,\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$
$\mathbf{w} \times 4\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} \times 3\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$
$\mathbf{w} \times (4\mathbf{v} + 3\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0}$
$\mathbf{w}$ is parallel to $3\mathbf{u} + 4\mathbf{v}$
$\therefore \mathbf{w} = \lambda(3\mathbf{u} + 4\mathbf{v})$

subparts.text: It is now given that $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are unit vectors which are perpendicular. Use a suitable scalar product to find the modulus of vector $\mathbf{w}$ in terms of $\lambda$.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$|\mathbf{w}|^2 = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{w} = \lambda(3\mathbf{u} + 4\mathbf{v}) \cdot \lambda(3\mathbf{u} + 4\mathbf{v})$
$= \lambda^2\left(9\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u} + 12\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + 12\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + 16\,\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}\right)$
$= \lambda^2\left(9|\mathbf{u}|^2 + 24\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + 16|\mathbf{v}|^2\right)$
$= \lambda^2\left(9(1)^2 + 24(0) + 16(1)^2\right) = \lambda^2(9 + 16) = 25\lambda^2$
$|\mathbf{w}| = 5|\lambda|$

parts.text: Referred to the origin $O$, points $A$, $B$ and $C$ have position vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ respectively. Point $C$ lies on line $AB$ produced such that $AC : AB = k : 1$, where $k$ is a constant and $1 < k < 2$. Show that $\mathbf{c} = (1 - k)\mathbf{a} + k\mathbf{b}$. $\;[1]$ $\;D$ is the mid-point of $OA$. The lines $DB$ produced and $OC$ produced meet at the point $E$. Given that $k = \dfrac{3}{2}$, find, in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, the position vector of $E$ and find the ratio $DB : DE$. $\;[4]$
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$\overrightarrow{AC} = k\,\overrightarrow{AB}$
$\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a} = k(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$
$\mathbf{c} = (1 - k)\mathbf{a} + k\mathbf{b}$ (shown)

Equation of line through $O$ and $C$: $\mathbf{r} = \lambda\mathbf{c}$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ $\quad(1)$
Equation of line through $D$ and $B$: $\mathbf{r} = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \mu\left(\mathbf{b} - \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}\right)$, $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ $\quad(2)$
Given $k = \dfrac{3}{2}$: $\mathbf{c} = \left(1 - \dfrac{3}{2}\right)\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{b} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{b}$ $\quad(4)$
Substitute $(4)$ into $(1) = (2)$:
$\lambda\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{b}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \mu\left(\mathbf{b} - \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}\right)$
Comparing $\mathbf{a}$: $-\dfrac{1}{2}\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\mu$ $\quad(5)$
Comparing $\mathbf{b}$: $\dfrac{3}{2}\lambda = \mu$ $\quad(6)$
Substitute $(6)$ into $(5)$: $-\dfrac{1}{2}\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{3}{4}\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda = 2$, $\therefore \mu = 3$
$\overrightarrow{OE} = 2\mathbf{c} = 2\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{b}\right) = -\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}$
$\overrightarrow{DE} = \overrightarrow{OE} - \overrightarrow{OD} = -\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b} - \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} = -\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b} = 3\left(\mathbf{b} - \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}\right) = 3\,\overrightarrow{DB}$
Therefore $DB : DE = 1 : 3$

parts.text: The cash price of a new laptop is $\$3369$. Ahmad buys this laptop on hire purchase. He pays a deposit of one third of the cash price followed by $36$ equal monthly instalments. The total amount Ahmad pays for the laptop is $\$3650.20$.

subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Total payable after deposit $= 3650.20 - \dfrac{3369}{3} = 2527.20$.
Monthly instalment $= \dfrac{2527.20}{36} = \$70.20$.

subparts.text: Calculate the simple interest rate per annum. [2]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Simple interest $= 3650.20 - 3369 = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{3} \times 3369 \times R \times \dfrac{36}{12}}{100}$.
Solving: $R = 4.17\%$ (to 3 s.f.).

The exchange rate between Singapore dollars ($\$$) and Chinese Yuan ($\yen$) is $\$1 = \yen 5.41$. Calculate the percentage savings by Catherine. [3]
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Price of laptop in Singapore dollars before tax $= \dfrac{15200}{5.41} = 2809.6118$.
Price after tax $= 2809.6118 \times 1.08 = 3034.3807$.
Percentage savings $= \dfrac{3369 - 3034.3807}{3369} \times 100\% = 9.93\%$ (to 3 s.f.).

parts.text: With reference to the Venn diagram below, $S$ is the universal set and $A$ and $B$ are non-empty proper subsets of $S$. Explain whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, and write down the value of $P(A \mid B)$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are independent, $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$.
Since $B \subset A$, $P(A \cap B) = P(B)$ and since $A \subset S$, $P(A) \neq 1$.
So $P(A \cap B) = P(B) \neq P(A)P(B)$. Hence $A$ and $B$ are not independent.
$P(A \mid B) = 1$

parts.text: A fair die has three sides numbered 2, two sides numbered 1 and one side numbered 0 . A game is played by throwing this fair die three times and the score, $X$, is the sum of the numbers obtained.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show that $P(X = 2) = \frac{7}{72}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$P(X = 2) = P($'2' appears once and '0' appears twice or '1' appears twice and '0' appears once$)$
$= \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{3!}{2!} + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{3!}{2!} = \frac{7}{72}$

subparts.text:
The table shows an incomplete probability distribution of $X$. Find the missing probabilities, showing your workings clearly. [3]
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & \frac{1}{216} & \frac{1}{36} & \frac{7}{72} & {} & \frac{7}{24} & {} & {} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$P(X = 6) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}$
$P(X = 5) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3!}{2!} = \frac{1}{4}$
$P(X = 3) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{6} \times 3! + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{11}{54}$

subparts.text:
The game is played 5 time
Find the probability that exactly one of the games obtained a score of 0 and exactly 2 games obtained a score of more than 2 .
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Required Probability $= P(X = 0) \times [P(X > 2)]^2 \times [P(X = 1 \text{ or } 2)]^2 \times \frac{5!}{2!2!}$
$= \frac{1}{216} \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{216} - \frac{1}{36} - \frac{7}{72}\right)^2 \times \left(\frac{1}{36} + \frac{7}{72}\right)^2 \times \frac{5!}{2!2!}$
$= 0.00164$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: Find the exterior angle of a regular octagon.

parts.solution:
Exterior angle $= \dfrac{360^\circ}{8} = 45^\circ$

Alternatively, interior angle $= \dfrac{(8 - 2) \times 180^\circ}{8} = 135^\circ$, so exterior angle $= 180^\circ - 135^\circ = 45^\circ$.

parts.text: The diagram shows three regular pentagons. Find the value of
parts.label: b

subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) Interior angle of a regular pentagon $= \dfrac{(5 - 2) \times 180^\circ}{5} = 108^\circ$, so $a = 108$.

(b) At the meeting point, two interior angles plus $b^\circ$ sum to $360^\circ$ (angles at a point):
$b^\circ = 360^\circ - 108^\circ - 108^\circ = 144^\circ$, so $b = 144$.

(c) The triangle at the top is isosceles, with apex angle $144^\circ$.
$m^\circ = \dfrac{180^\circ - 144^\circ}{2} = 18^\circ$, so $m = 18$.

subparts.text: Additional pentagons are added to the three pentagons to form a closed ring which is in the shape of a regular polygon. Find the number of additional pentagons needed to form the closed ring.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
The closed ring is a regular polygon whose interior angle equals $144^\circ$ (the gap angle $b$).

$\dfrac{(n - 2) \times 180^\circ}{n} = 144^\circ$

$180n - 360 = 144n$

$36n = 360 \Rightarrow n = 10$

Number of additional pentagons $= 10 - 3 = 7$

$$\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{r}{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)} = A\left[\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{n+2} - \frac{3}{n+3}\right]$$
where $A$ is a constant to be determined. Explain why $\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{r}{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)}$ is a convergent series, and state the value of the sum to infinity. [6]
In the diagram, $AC = 10$ cm, $BC = 5$ cm and $AB = x$ cm. It is also given that $\sin\angle ACB = \frac{3}{5}$.

parts.text:
Find
(a) the value of $\cos\angle ACB$, leaving your answer in fraction, [1]
(b) the exact value of $x^{2}$. [2]
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
(a) From the diagram $\angle ACB$ is acute, so $\cos\angle ACB$ is positive.
$\cos\angle ACB = \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} = \frac{4}{5}$
(b) By the cosine rule,
$x^{2} = AC^{2} + BC^{2} - 2(AC)(BC)\cos\angle ACB$
$x^{2} = 10^{2} + 5^{2} - 2(10)(5)\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)$
$x^{2} = 100 + 25 - 80$
$x^{2} = 45$

parts.text: Hence find the exact value of $\sin\angle BAC$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$AB = x = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}$
By the sine rule,
$\frac{\sin\angle BAC}{BC} = \frac{\sin\angle ACB}{AB}$
$\sin\angle BAC = \frac{5 \times \frac{3}{5}}{3\sqrt{5}}$
$= \frac{3}{3\sqrt{5}}$
$= \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$

subparts.text: Find angle $AFB$. Give a reason for each step of your working. [2]

subparts.solution:

$\angle AFB = 180^\circ - 36^\circ - 56^\circ = 88^\circ$ ($\angle$ sum of $\triangle$).

parts.text: In the diagram, $TA$ and $TB$ are tangents to the circle at $A$ and $B$ respectively. $D$ is a point on the circle such that $BD$ is parallel to $TA$. $C$ is a point inside the circle such that angle $CBD$ is $18^\circ$. Angle $ATB$ is $62^\circ$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Find angle $TAB$. Give a reason for your working. [1]
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Angle $TAB = 59^\circ$ (base angles of isosceles triangle $TAB$ with $TA = TB$).
subparts.solution:
$TA = TB$ (equal tangents from external point).
$\angle TAB = (180^\circ - 62^\circ) \div 2 = 59^\circ$ (base $\angle s$ of isosceles $\triangle$).

subparts.text: Show that $C$ is not the centre of the circle. [2]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Shown: If $C$ were the centre, $CB = CD$ (radii), making triangle $BCD$ isosceles with $\angle CDB = \angle CBD = 18^\circ$. But using alternate segment/parallel line properties, the angle $\angle CDB$ must be $59^\circ$, which contradicts $18^\circ$. Hence $C$ is not the centre.
subparts.solution:
$\angle TBC = 180^\circ - 62^\circ - 18^\circ = 100^\circ$ (int. $\angle s$, $TA \parallel BD$).
By the property `radius $\perp$ tangent', as $\angle TBC \neq 90^\circ$, $BC$ is not a radius of the circle.
Hence $C$ is not the centre of the circle.

Is it feasible to construct such a roof? Justify your answer. [2]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Equation of plane $STUV$: $\mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = 16$. By observation, $(16, 0, 0)$ lies on the plane $STUV$. Since $OP = 20$ m, it is not feasible to build such a roof. Alternatively, $\overrightarrow{OT} = \begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \\ x \end{pmatrix}$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \\ x \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = 16$, so $x = -2$; it is impossible to build the roof as one edge would have to be underground.

parts.text: Using the distribution you have stated, find the probability that a randomly chosen packet of 10 balloons contains an equal number of oval balloons and round balloons.
parts.label: i

parts.text: Using the distribution you have stated, find the probability that a randomly chosen packet of 10 balloons contains at least 3 but not more than 5 oval balloons.
parts.label: ii

parts.text: A box consists of $m$ randomly chosen packets of 10 balloons. Find the least value of $m$ such that there is at least $0.95$ probability that a randomly chosen box contains at least 1 packet of balloons with an equal number of oval balloons and round balloons.
parts.label: iii

stem:
The position vector of the point $A$ is $2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k}$, and the equation of the line $l$ is $\mathbf{r} = -7\mathbf{i} + 15\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k} + \lambda\left(3\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}\right)$.
Find the position vectors of the points $B$ and $C$, both lying on $l$, such that $AB = AC = 10$. [3]
Given that the point $P$ is the midpoint of $BC$, show that the equation of the plane $\Pi_{1}$, which contains $l$ and is perpendicular to $AP$, is $\mathbf{r} \cdot \left(-3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}\right) = \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is an integer to be determined. [2]
The planes $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$ have equations $\mathbf{r} \cdot \left(\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}\right) = 5$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot \left(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right) = 1$ respectively, and $A$ lies in both $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$.

parts.text: Determine the position vector of $D$, the point of intersection between $\Pi_{1}$, $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
First the two results demanded in the stem.
A general point of $l$ is $\begin{pmatrix} -7 + 3\lambda \\ 15 - 7\lambda \\ -5 + 4\lambda \end{pmatrix}$, so $\overrightarrow{AX} = \begin{pmatrix} -9 + 3\lambda \\ 15 - 7\lambda \\ -4 + 4\lambda \end{pmatrix}$ and
$\left|\overrightarrow{AX}\right|^{2} = 74\lambda^{2} - 296\lambda + 322 = 100 \Rightarrow \lambda^{2} - 4\lambda + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1 \text{ or } 3$.
$\lambda = 1$: $\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 8 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$; $\lambda = 3$: $\overrightarrow{OC} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -6 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$.
$P$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $\overrightarrow{OP} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AP} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$.
$\overrightarrow{AP} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -7 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = -9 - 7 + 16 = 0$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}$ is perpendicular to $l$ and is a normal of $\Pi_{1}$; using the point $(-7,\ 15,\ -5)$ of $l$,
$\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} -7 \\ 15 \\ -5 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = 21 + 15 - 20 = 16$.
Now solve the three plane equations simultaneously:
$-3x + y + 4z = 16$, $x + 2y - 3z = 5$, $x - 2y + z = 1$.
Solving (e.g. with the GC) gives $x = 15$, $y = 13$, $z = 12$, so $\overrightarrow{OD} = \begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 13 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$.

parts.text: Hence find the volume of the tetrahedron $ABCD$. $\left[\text{Volume of tetrahedron} = \frac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times \text{height}\right]$
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Take triangle $ABC$ as the base. With $A(2,\ 0,\ -1)$,
$\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 8 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -6 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 64 \\ 48 \\ 36 \end{pmatrix}$.
Base area $= \frac{1}{2}\left|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}\right| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{7696} = 43.863$ units$^2$.
A unit normal to plane $ABC$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{481}}\begin{pmatrix} 16 \\ 12 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$, so the height is
$\left|\overrightarrow{AD} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{481}}\left|\begin{pmatrix} 13 \\ 13 \\ 13 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 16 \\ 12 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}\right| = \frac{481}{\sqrt{481}} = \sqrt{481} = 21.932$ units.
Volume $= \frac{1}{3} \times 43.863 \times 21.932 = 320.67 \approx 321$ units$^3$.
(Equivalently $\frac{1}{6}\left|\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \left(\overrightarrow{AC} \times \overrightarrow{AD}\right)\right| = \frac{1924}{6} = 320.67$.)

subparts.solution:

Bearing of $C$ from $B = 136.608^\circ - 90^\circ = 046.6^\circ$ (to 1 d.p.).

subparts.solution:
Shortest distance from $B$ to line $CD$ $= \dfrac{412.55}{\dfrac{1}{2} \times 46} = 17.936$ m.

$$\sum a = 400\,000, \quad \sum a^2 = 4\,002\,246\,400$$

parts.text: Calculate the unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance. [2]
parts.label: i

The diagram shows Solid A consisting of a right circular cone attached to a hemisphere with a common circular base of radius $r$ cm. The height of the cone is $24$ cm. The volume of the cone is equal to twice the volume of the hemisphere.

parts.text: Show that $r = 6$. [2]
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cone $= 2 \times$ Volume of hemisphere
$\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 (24) = 2 \times \dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3$
$24 = 4r$
$r = 6$. (Shown.)

parts.text: Solid $\mathbf{B}$ is constructed by removing a smaller cone of base radius $x$ cm and height $y$ cm.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Find the value of $\dfrac{x}{y}$. [1]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: By similar triangles, $\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{6}{24} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ or $\dfrac{x}{6} = \dfrac{y}{24}$.

subparts.text: Given that the volume of the cone removed is $121.5\pi$ cm$^3$, calculate the total surface area of Solid B. [5]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{1}{4} \Rightarrow y = 4x$.
$\dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^2 y = 121.5\pi \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^2 (4x) = 121.5\pi \Rightarrow x^3 = \dfrac{729}{8} \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{9}{2}$.
Slant height of big cone $= \sqrt{24^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{612}$.
Slant height of small cone $= \sqrt{18^2 + (9/2)^2} = \sqrt{344.25}$.
Curved surface area of remaining solid $= \pi(6)(\sqrt{612}) - \pi(9/2)(\sqrt{344.25}) = 204.01$.
Curved surface area of hemisphere $= 2\pi(6)^2 = 72\pi$.
Total surface area $= 72\pi + \pi(9/2)^2 + 204.01 = 494$ cm$^2$ (to 3 s.f.).

stem:
Given that $y=\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]$, show that
$$\cos y\,\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{x+1} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \cos y\,\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-\sin y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}=-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}.$$
[2]

parts.text: By further differentiation, find the Maclaurin series for $y$, up to and including the term in $x^{3}$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
From $y=\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]$ we have $\sin y=\ln(x+1)$; differentiating gives $\cos y\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}$, and differentiating again gives
$$\cos y\,\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-\sin y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}=-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}.$$
Differentiating once more:
$$\cos y\,\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}-3\sin y\,\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-\cos y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3}=\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}}.$$
At $x=0$: $\sin y=\ln 1=0$, so $y=0$ and $\cos y=1$.
From the first equation: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$.
From the second: $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-0=-1$, so $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-1$.
From the third: $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}-0-1=2$, so $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}=3$.
Hence
$$y=0+x+\frac{-1}{2!}x^{2}+\frac{3}{3!}x^{3}+\cdots=x-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x^{3}+\cdots$$

parts.text: Find the set of values of $x$ for which the value of $y$ is within $\pm 0.1$ of the value found by its Maclaurin series.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Require
$$\left|\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]-\left(x-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x^{3}\right)\right|<0.1.$$
The function $y$ is defined only where $-1 \leq \ln(x+1) \leq 1$, i.e. $e^{-1}-1 \leq x \leq e-1$.
Using a graphic calculator to sketch $\left|y-\left(x-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x^{3}\right)\right|$ and $y=0.1$, the curves meet at $x=-0.521$ and $x=0.783$ (3 s.f.).
Hence the required set is $\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -0.521<x<0.783\right\}$.

parts.text: Deduce the series expansion for $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}}}$ up to and including the term in $x^{2}$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Since $\sin y=\ln(x+1)$ and $y=\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]$ lies in $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, we have $\cos y=\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}} \geq 0$.
From $\cos y\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}$,
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}}}.$$
Differentiating the series in part (i) term by term:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=1-x+\frac{3}{2}x^{2}+\cdots$$
Hence $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}}}=1-x+\dfrac{3}{2}x^{2}+\cdots$

parts.answer:

stem: Evaluate the following integrals.

parts.text: By using the substitution $x = \frac{1}{t}$, find $\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}\,dx$ leaving your answer in exact form.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let $x = \frac{1}{t}$, so $dx = -\frac{1}{t^{2}}\,dt$.
When $x = \sqrt{2}$, $t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$; when $x = 2$, $t = \frac{1}{2}$.
For $t > 0$, $\sqrt{x^{2} - 1} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{t^{2}} - 1} = \frac{\sqrt{1 - t^{2}}}{t}$.
$\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}dx = \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{1}{\frac{1}{t}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}{t}}\left(-\frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)dt$
$= \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{t^{2}}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}\left(-\frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)dt$
$= -\int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}dt$
$= -\left[\sin^{-1}t\right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}$
$= -\left(\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$
$= \frac{\pi}{12}$

parts.text:
Show that $\int\frac{x + 1}{x^{2} + 4x + 7}dx = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(x^{2} + 4x + 7\right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{x + 2}{\sqrt{3}} + c$. [4]

Hence find $\int_{-2}^{1}\frac{\left| x + 1 \right|}{x^{2} + 4x + 7}dx$ exactly. [3]
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Write $x + 1 = \frac{1}{2}(2x + 4) - 1$, and note $x^{2} + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)^{2} + 3$.
$\int\frac{x+1}{x^{2}+4x+7}dx = \frac{1}{2}\int\frac{2x+4}{x^{2}+4x+7}dx - \int\frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}+3}dx$
$= \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(x^{2}+4x+7\right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{3}} + c$ (shown)

For the definite integral, $\left|x+1\right| = -(x+1)$ on $[-2,\ -1]$ and $x+1$ on $[-1,\ 1]$.
Let $F(x) = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(x^{2}+4x+7\right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{3}}$.
$F(-2) = \frac{1}{2}\ln 3 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}0 = \frac{1}{2}\ln 3$
$F(-1) = \frac{1}{2}\ln 4 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \ln 2 - \frac{\pi}{6\sqrt{3}}$
$F(1) = \frac{1}{2}\ln 12 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = \frac{1}{2}\ln 12 - \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}$
$\int_{-2}^{1}\frac{|x+1|}{x^{2}+4x+7}dx = -\left[F(-1) - F(-2)\right] + \left[F(1) - F(-1)\right]$
$= \left(\frac{1}{2}\ln 3 - \ln 2 + \frac{\pi}{6\sqrt{3}}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{2}\ln 12 - \ln 2 - \frac{\pi}{6\sqrt{3}}\right)$
The $\tan^{-1}$ terms cancel:
$= \frac{1}{2}\ln 36 - 2\ln 2 = \ln 6 - \ln 4 = \ln\frac{3}{2}$

parts.text:
The masses, in grams, of $200$ apples of each of variety A and variety B are recorded.
The cumulative frequency curves show the distributions of their masses.
parts.label: a

subparts.text:
Use the curve to estimate

(a) the median mass for variety A, **[1]**

(b) the $60$th percentile for variety B, **[1]**

(c) the interquartile range for variety B. **[2]**
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) The median is the $100$th value. Read across from a cumulative frequency of $100$ to the variety A curve, then down to the mass axis.

Median mass for variety A $= 94$ g

(b) $60\%$ of $200 = 120$. Read across from a cumulative frequency of $120$ to the variety B curve.

$60$th percentile for variety B $= 106$ g

(c) Lower quartile: read at a cumulative frequency of $\dfrac{1}{4} \times 200 = 50$, giving $Q_1 = 87$ g.

Upper quartile: read at a cumulative frequency of $\dfrac{3}{4} \times 200 = 150$, giving $Q_3 = 114$ g.

Interquartile range $= 114 - 87 = 27$ g

subparts.text:
George sells apples in packs of $6$.
He uses apples with a mass between $80$ g and $120$ g and rejects the rest.

Which variety of apples would be better for George to use?
Justify your answer using appropriate figures.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Variety A, since $180 - 24 = 156$ of the variety A apples have a mass between $80$ g and $120$ g, compared with $164 - 32 = 132$ of the variety B apples.
subparts.solution:
Variety A: at $120$ g the cumulative frequency is $180$; at $80$ g it is $24$.

Number George can use $= 180 - 24 = 156$

subparts.text:
Two apples are taken from the box at random, without replacement.

Find, as a fraction in its simplest form, the probability that the two apples are the same variety.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$P(\text{same variety}) = P(AA) + P(BB)$

$= \dfrac{9}{16} \times \dfrac{8}{15} + \dfrac{7}{16} \times \dfrac{6}{15}$

$= \dfrac{72}{240} + \dfrac{42}{240}$

$= \dfrac{114}{240} = \dfrac{19}{40}$

subparts.text:
These two apples are returned to the box and $4$ apples of variety C are also added to the box.
Three apples are taken from the box, at random, without replacement.

Find, as a fraction in its simplest form, the probability that two out of the three apples are of variety C.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
The box now holds $9 + 7 + 4 = 20$ apples, of which $4$ are variety C.

$P(\text{exactly two of variety C}) = \dfrac{\binom{4}{2} \times \binom{16}{1}}{\binom{20}{3}}$

$= \dfrac{6 \times 16}{1140} = \dfrac{96}{1140} = \dfrac{8}{95}$

parts.text:
On a single Argand diagram, sketch the loci

(a) $z = \dfrac{4}{z^{*}}$,\ \ [3]

(b) $|z+2| = \left|z - 1 + i\sqrt3\right|$.\ \ [3]
parts.label: iii
parts.answer: (a) the circle centre $O$, radius $2$; (b) the straight line $y = \sqrt3\,x$ (the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining $(-2,\,0)$ and $(1,\,-\sqrt3)$).
parts.solution:
**(a)** From part (i) the equation is equivalent to $|z| = 2$: a **circle with centre the origin and radius $2$**.

**(b)** Write the equation as
$$\left|z - (-2)\right| = \left|z - \left(1 - i\sqrt3\right)\right| ,$$
so the locus is the **perpendicular bisector** of the segment joining $A(-2,\,0)$ and $B\left(1,\,-\sqrt3\right)$.

Midpoint of $AB$: $\left(-\tfrac12,\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Gradient of $AB$: $\dfrac{-\sqrt3 - 0}{1 - (-2)} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so the perpendicular bisector has gradient $\sqrt3$:
$$y + \frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \sqrt3\left(x + \frac12\right) \;\Longrightarrow\; y = \sqrt3\,x .$$

The two loci are sketched on one Argand diagram: the circle $|z|=2$ and the line $y = \sqrt3 x$ through the origin, which cuts the circle at two points.

parts.text: The complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$ satisfy the equations $z = \dfrac{4}{z^{*}}$ and $|z+2| = \left|z - 1 + i\sqrt3\right|$, where $\arg(z_1) > \arg(z_2)$. Find the exact values of $z_1$ and $z_2$, giving your answers in the form $x + iy$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
$z_1$ and $z_2$ are the intersections of the two loci, i.e. of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ with the line $y = \sqrt3\,x$:
$$x^2 + 3x^2 = 4 \;\Longrightarrow\; 4x^2 = 4 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = \pm 1 .$$
So the points are $\left(1,\ \sqrt3\right)$ and $\left(-1,\ -\sqrt3\right)$, i.e. $1 + \sqrt3\,i$ and $-1 - \sqrt3\,i$.

Their arguments are
$$\arg\!\left(1 + \sqrt3\,i\right) = \frac{\pi}{3}, \qquad \arg\!\left(-1 - \sqrt3\,i\right) = -\frac{2\pi}{3} ,$$
and $\dfrac{\pi}{3} > -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so
$$\boxed{z_1 = 1 + \sqrt3\,i, \qquad z_2 = -1 - \sqrt3\,i}$$

parts.text: Another complex number $w$ satisfies $w = \dfrac{4}{w^{*}}$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}\pi < \arg(w) < \pi$. Explain why $\arg(z_1 - w) - \arg(z_2 - w) = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$.
parts.label: v
parts.answer: Since $z_2 = -z_1$, the chord $z_1z_2$ is a diameter of the circle $|z| = 2$, on which $w$ also lies; the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so the angle between $z_1 - w$ and $z_2 - w$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
parts.solution:
$w$ also satisfies $w = \dfrac{4}{w^{*}}$, so by part (i) $|w| = 2$: $w$ lies on the same circle as $z_1$ and $z_2$ (and $\tfrac12\pi < \arg w < \pi$ puts $w$ in the second quadrant, so $w \ne z_1,\,z_2$).

Since $z_2 = -z_1$, the points $z_1$ and $z_2$ are diametrically opposite, so the chord $z_1z_2$ is a **diameter** of the circle. The vectors $z_1 - w$ and $z_2 - w$ are the two chords from $w$ to the ends of that diameter, and the **angle in a semicircle is a right angle**, so the angle between them is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Taking directions into account (with $w$ in the second quadrant, $z_1$ in the first and $z_2$ in the third),
$$\arg(z_1 - w) - \arg(z_2 - w) = \frac{\pi}{2} .$$
*Check with $w = 2e^{i2\pi/3} = -1 + \sqrt3 i$:* $z_1 - w = 2$ (argument $0$) and $z_2 - w = -2\sqrt3\,i$ (argument $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$), giving a difference of $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. $\checkmark$

Since $\sec^{2}\theta = 1 + \tan^{2}\theta$ and $y = \tan\left(e^{x}-1\right)$,
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(1 + \tan^{2}\left(e^{x}-1\right)\right)e^{x} = \left(1 + y^{2}\right)e^{x}\quad\blacksquare$$

$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{dy}{dx}\left(1 + 2e^{x}y\right)$.

Find the Maclaurin's series for $y$, up to and including the term in $x^{2}$. [2]

parts.solution:
Differentiating $\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(1+y^{2}\right)e^{x}$ with respect to $x$ (product rule):
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \left(2y\frac{dy}{dx}\right)e^{x} + \left(1+y^{2}\right)e^{x}$$
$$= 2ye^{x}\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{dx}\left(1 + 2e^{x}y\right)\quad\blacksquare$$

When $x = 0$: $y = \tan\left(e^{0}-1\right) = \tan 0 = 0$.
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(1 + 0^{2}\right)e^{0} = 1$.
$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = 1\left(1 + 2(1)(0)\right) = 1$.

$$y = y(0) + \frac{dy}{dx}\bigg|_{0}x + \frac{1}{2!}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\bigg|_{0}x^{2} + \ldots = x + \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + \ldots$$

A function $f$ is said to be odd if $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain of $f$.

The function $h$ is defined by

$$h: x \longmapsto \frac{x^{2}+k^{2}}{x},\quad x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \neq 0,$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

parts.text: Show that $h$ is an odd function. If $g$ is also an odd function, determine with a reason, whether the function $gh$ is an odd function.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$$h(-x) = \frac{(-x)^{2}+k^{2}}{-x} = -\frac{x^{2}+k^{2}}{x} = -h(x)$$
so $h$ is odd. $\blacksquare$

$$gh(-x) = g\left(h(-x)\right) = g\left(-h(x)\right) = -g\left(h(x)\right) = -gh(x)$$
using that $h$ is odd and then that $g$ is odd. Hence $gh$ is an odd function.

parts.text: Without using a calculator, find the set of values that $h(x)$ can take.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Let $y = \frac{x^{2}+k^{2}}{x}$. Then $x^{2} - yx + k^{2} = 0$.

For real $x$ the discriminant must be non-negative:
$$y^{2} - 4k^{2} \geq 0 \Rightarrow (y-2k)(y+2k) \geq 0 \Rightarrow y \leq -2k \text{ or } y \geq 2k$$
(the excluded value $x = 0$ would require $k^{2} = 0$, which is impossible since $k > 0$).

$$R_{h} = \{\,y \in \mathbb{R} : y \leq -2k \text{ or } y \geq 2k\,\}$$

parts.text:
Sketch the curve $y = h(x)$, stating the equations of any asymptotes and the coordinates of any stationary points.

Hence find the range of values of $m$ such that the equation $\frac{x^{2}+k^{2}}{x} = mx + 2k$ has two distinct real roots. [1]
parts.label: iii
parts.answer: Asymptotes $x = 0$ and $y = x$; stationary points $(k,\ 2k)$ and $(-k,\ -2k)$;  $m > 0$, $m \neq 1$
parts.solution:
$$h(x) = x + \frac{k^{2}}{x}$$
Asymptotes: $x = 0$ (vertical) and $y = x$ (oblique).

$$h'(x) = 1 - \frac{k^{2}}{x^{2}} = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm k$$
Stationary points: $(k,\ 2k)$ — a minimum — and $(-k,\ -2k)$ — a maximum.

The curve has two branches: one in the first quadrant above $y = 2k$, one in the third quadrant below $y = -2k$, each approaching $x = 0$ and $y = x$.

For the equation $\frac{x^{2}+k^{2}}{x} = mx + 2k$:
$$x^{2} + k^{2} = mx^{2} + 2kx \Rightarrow (1-m)x^{2} - 2kx + k^{2} = 0$$

If $m = 1$: $-2kx + k^{2} = 0$ gives the single root $x = \frac{k}{2}$ — rejected.

If $m \neq 1$, two distinct real roots require
$$(-2k)^{2} - 4(1-m)k^{2} > 0 \Rightarrow 4k^{2}\left[1 - (1-m)\right] > 0 \Rightarrow 4k^{2}m > 0 \Rightarrow m > 0$$

$$\therefore\ m > 0,\ m \neq 1$$

stem: Referred to the origin $O$, the position vectors of the points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are $\mathbf{p}$, $\mathbf{q}$ and $\mathbf{r}$ respectively.

parts.text: Given that the point $R$ divides $PQ$ externally in the ratio $4 : 3$, show that the length of the projection of $\overrightarrow{OR}$ onto $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is given by $\left|\frac{4\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}}{\left|\mathbf{p}\right|} - 3\left|\mathbf{p}\right|\right|$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$R$ divides $PQ$ externally in the ratio $4:3$, so by the ratio theorem
$$\mathbf{r} = \frac{4\mathbf{q} - 3\mathbf{p}}{4 - 3} = 4\mathbf{q} - 3\mathbf{p}$$

Length of projection of $\overrightarrow{OR}$ onto $\overrightarrow{OP}$:
$$\left|\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}}\right| = \frac{\left|\left(4\mathbf{q}-3\mathbf{p}\right)\cdot\mathbf{p}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{p}\right|} = \frac{\left|4(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}) - 3\left|\mathbf{p}\right|^{2}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{p}\right|}$$
$$= \left|\frac{4\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}}{\left|\mathbf{p}\right|} - 3\left|\mathbf{p}\right|\right|\quad\blacksquare$$

parts.text:
Given that the point $R$ divides $PQ$ internally in the ratio $a : b$, show that $\frac{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{q}} = \frac{b\left|\mathbf{p}\right|^{2} + a\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)}{a\left|\mathbf{q}\right|^{2} + b\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)}$.

Deduce that, when the line $OR$ bisects angle $POQ$, then $a : b = \left|\mathbf{p}\right| : \left|\mathbf{q}\right|$. [3]
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
By the ratio theorem, $\mathbf{r} = \frac{b\mathbf{p} + a\mathbf{q}}{a+b}$.

$$\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p} = \frac{b\left|\mathbf{p}\right|^{2} + a\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)}{a+b},\qquad \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{q} = \frac{b\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right) + a\left|\mathbf{q}\right|^{2}}{a+b}$$

$$\frac{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{q}} = \frac{b\left|\mathbf{p}\right|^{2} + a\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)}{a\left|\mathbf{q}\right|^{2} + b\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)}\quad\blacksquare$$

If $OR$ bisects angle $POQ$, the angle between $\mathbf{r}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ equals the angle between $\mathbf{r}$ and $\mathbf{q}$, so
$$\frac{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}}{\left|\mathbf{r}\right|\left|\mathbf{p}\right|} = \frac{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{q}}{\left|\mathbf{r}\right|\left|\mathbf{q}\right|} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{q}} = \frac{\left|\mathbf{p}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{q}\right|}$$

$$\frac{b\left|\mathbf{p}\right|^{2} + a\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)}{a\left|\mathbf{q}\right|^{2} + b\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)} = \frac{\left|\mathbf{p}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{q}\right|}$$
$$b\left|\mathbf{p}\right|^{2}\left|\mathbf{q}\right| + a\left|\mathbf{q}\right|\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right) = a\left|\mathbf{p}\right|\left|\mathbf{q}\right|^{2} + b\left|\mathbf{p}\right|\left(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)$$
$$b\left|\mathbf{p}\right|\left(\left|\mathbf{p}\right|\left|\mathbf{q}\right| - \mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right) = a\left|\mathbf{q}\right|\left(\left|\mathbf{p}\right|\left|\mathbf{q}\right| - \mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)$$

Since $P$, $O$, $Q$ are not collinear, $\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q} \neq \left|\mathbf{p}\right|\left|\mathbf{q}\right|$, so the bracket may be cancelled:
$$b\left|\mathbf{p}\right| = a\left|\mathbf{q}\right| \Rightarrow \frac{a}{b} = \frac{\left|\mathbf{p}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{q}\right|} \Rightarrow a : b = \left|\mathbf{p}\right| : \left|\mathbf{q}\right|\quad\blacksquare$$
