$\dfrac{d^2C}{dp^2} = 2.8 - 12p$; when $p = 0.62633$, $\dfrac{d^2C}{dp^2} = 2.8 - 7.516 = -4.72 < 0$,

so this value of $p$ gives a maximum.

$\therefore C$ is maximum when $p = 0.626$ (3 s.f.)

stem:
The stress level and job performance of a company's employees are measured using the stress index and job performance index that a human resource consultant developed. The consultant is investigating the relationship between the stress level of an employee and his job performance. The data of 8 employees is tabulated as follows.
$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Stress level, } x & 2.5 & 3.13 & 3.75 & 4.38 & 5 & 6.25 & 7.5 & 8.75 \\ \hline \text{Job Performance, } y & 4.20 & 3.75 & 3.56 & 3.40 & 3.23 & 3.09 & 3.03 & 2.97 \\ \hline \end{array}$

parts.text: Draw a scatter diagram for the data and calculate the product moment correlation coefficient between $y$ and $x$. [3]
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
The scatter diagram is plotted with $x$ (stress level) on the horizontal axis, from $2.5$ to $8.75$, and $y$ (job performance) on the vertical axis, from $2.97$ to $4.20$.

The points fall steeply at first and then flatten out, decreasing throughout and curving towards a horizontal level.

Using the GC (LinReg / 2-variable statistics):

$r = -0.90109 = -0.901$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: Explain whether a linear model is appropriate. [1]
parts.label: ii
parts.answer: A linear model is not appropriate, as the points on the scatter diagram do not follow a linear trend — $y$ decreases at a decreasing rate.
parts.solution:
Although $r = -0.901$ is fairly close to $-1$, the scatter diagram shows that the points do not lie close to a straight line: as $x$ increases, $y$ decreases at a $\textit{decreasing}$ rate, so the trend is curved and appears to level off.

A linear model is therefore $\textbf{not}$ appropriate for this data.

parts.text: Observing the general trend of the points in the scatter diagram, the consultant proposes that a model of the form $y = \dfrac{a}{x} + b$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants is more appropriate. Evaluate the consultant's proposal. [1]
parts.label: iii
parts.answer: The proposal is appropriate: $r$ between $y$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ is $0.995$, closer to 1 in magnitude than $|-0.901|$.
parts.solution:
The product moment correlation coefficient between $y$ and $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is

$r = 0.99473 \approx 0.995$

Since $|0.995| > |-0.901|$, the linear relationship between $y$ and $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is stronger than that between $y$ and $x$.

The shape of the scatter diagram (decreasing, concave upwards, levelling off towards a positive value $b$) is also consistent with a model of the form $y = \dfrac{a}{x} + b$ with $a, b > 0$.

The consultant's proposal is therefore appropriate.

parts.text: Calculate the least-squares regression line of $y$ on $\dfrac{1}{x}$. [1]
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Using the GC to perform a linear regression of $y$ on $\dfrac{1}{x}$:

$y = 4.27835\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) + 2.42931$

$y = 4.2784\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) + 2.43$ (to 3 d.p. / 3 s.f.)

parts.text: Using the least-squares regression line in part (iv), estimate the job performance level of an employee when his stress level is 4. Comment on the reliability of the estimate. [2]
parts.label: v
parts.solution:
When $x = 4$, $\dfrac{1}{x} = 0.25$:

$y = 4.27835(0.25) + 2.42931 = 1.06959 + 2.42931 = 3.4989$

$y = 3.50$ (3 s.f.)

$\textbf{Reliability}$: the estimate is reliable, because

1. $x = 4$ lies within the range of the given data ($2.5 \leq x \leq 8.75$), so this is $\textbf{interpolation}$; and
2. $|r| = 0.995$ between $y$ and $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is very close to 1, indicating a strong linear relationship between $y$ and $\dfrac{1}{x}$.

parts.text:
The Traffic Authority claims that the average speed of vehicles along a road is at most 70 km per hour. The speed, $x$ km per hour, of 20 randomly selected vehicles are recorded and summarised as follows:
$$\sum(x - 70) = 71, \qquad \sum(x - 70)^2 = 1122$$
It is assumed that the speed of the vehicles is normally distributed.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Find the unbiased estimates of the mean and variance of the speed of vehicles along the road. [2]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let $y = x - 70$, with $n = 20$, $\sum y = 71$ and $\sum y^2 = 1122$.

$\textbf{Unbiased estimate of the mean}$

$\overline{x} = 70 + \dfrac{\sum(x-70)}{n} = 70 + \dfrac{71}{20} = 70 + 3.55 = 73.55$

$\textbf{Unbiased estimate of the variance}$

$s^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1}\left[\sum(x-70)^2 - \dfrac{\left(\sum(x-70)\right)^2}{n}\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{19}\left[1122 - \dfrac{71^2}{20}\right] = \dfrac{1}{19}\left[1122 - \dfrac{5041}{20}\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{19}\left[1122 - 252.05\right] = \dfrac{869.95}{19} = 45.787$

$s^2 = 45.8$ (3 s.f.)

subparts.text: Test, at 5% significance level, the Traffic Authority's claim. [4]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: $p$-value $= 0.0150 < 0.05$, so reject $H_0$: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean speed exceeds 70 km/h, so the claim is not supported.
subparts.solution:
Let $\mu$ be the population mean speed of vehicles along the road, in km per hour.

$H_0: \mu = 70$
$H_1: \mu > 70$

(The claim is that the mean is $\textit{at most}$ 70, so we test against the alternative that it is greater.)

Level of significance: 5%.

Since the population variance is unknown and the sample size $n = 20$ is small, but the speeds are assumed to be normally distributed, we use a $t$-test.

Under $H_0$, the test statistic is
$T = \dfrac{\overline{X} - 70}{s/\sqrt{n}} \sim t(19)$

$t = \dfrac{73.55 - 70}{\sqrt{45.787/20}} = \dfrac{3.55}{1.51306} = 2.3462$

From the GC, $p\text{-value} = P(T > 2.3462) = 0.01498 = 0.0150$ (3 s.f.)

Since $p\text{-value} = 0.0150 < 0.05$, we reject $H_0$.

There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level of significance to conclude that the mean speed of vehicles along the road is greater than 70 km per hour. The Traffic Authority's claim is not valid.

parts.text: In XYZ School, the students' mean running time in the 2.4 km run is claimed to be 705 seconds. A programme to help the students perform better in the run is introduced. After the programme, a sample of 100 students was taken and their mean running time is 690 seconds. At a significance level of 7%, a $z$-test was done to test if the students are performing better. It was concluded that there is sufficient evidence that the students are performing better in the 2.4 km run.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: In the test above, explain if any assumption about the students' 2.4 km running times is necessary. [1]
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: No assumption is necessary: the sample size of 100 is large, so by the Central Limit Theorem the sample mean is approximately normally distributed.
subparts.solution:
No assumption about the distribution of the students' running times is necessary.

The sample size $n = 100$ is large, so by the Central Limit Theorem the distribution of the sample mean running time is approximately normal regardless of the distribution of the underlying population.

This is what justifies the use of a $z$-test.

subparts.text: If a two-tailed test had been conducted, is it necessarily true, necessarily false or not necessarily true or false that the conclusion will remain the same? [2]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
For the one-tailed test, the $p$-value was less than $0.07$ (since $H_0$ was rejected).

For a two-tailed test using the same data, the $p$-value is exactly $\textbf{double}$ the one-tailed $p$-value.

Let the one-tailed $p$-value be $q$, so $q < 0.07$. The two-tailed $p$-value is $2q$.

If $q < 0.035$, then $2q < 0.07$ and $H_0$ would still be rejected — the conclusion would remain the same.
If $0.035 < q < 0.07$, then $2q > 0.07$ and $H_0$ would not be rejected — the conclusion would change.

Since we are not told the actual $p$-value, it is $\textbf{not necessarily true or false}$ that the conclusion will remain the same.

subparts.text: What can you do to increase the $p$-value in the test in part (b)? [1]
subparts.label: iii
subparts.answer: Decrease the claimed mean running time stated in $H_0$ (bring it closer to 690 seconds).
subparts.solution:
The $p$-value is $P\left(\overline{X} < 690\right)$ computed under $H_0: \mu = 705$.

Decreasing the claimed mean running time $\mu_0$ in $H_0$ moves it closer to the observed sample mean of 690 seconds, which reduces the magnitude of the test statistic $z = \dfrac{690 - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{100}}$ and therefore increases the $p$-value.

So: decrease the claimed mean running time.

stem:
A fruit stall sells 2 types of durians, XO and D24. For each type of durian, a randomly chosen durian has a mass that is normally distributed with mean and standard deviation, as well as unit price as shown in the following table.
$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline & \text{Mean (kg)} & \text{Standard deviation (kg)} & \text{Price per kg} \\ \hline \text{XO} & 2.5 & 0.8 & \$12 \\ \hline \text{D24} & 2.0 & 0.5 & \$7 \\ \hline \end{array}$

parts.text: Find the probability that the total mass of 2 randomly chosen XO durians is more than 3 times the mass of a randomly chosen D24 durian. [3]
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Let $X$ be the mass in kg of a randomly chosen XO durian, and $D$ that of a randomly chosen D24 durian.

$X \sim N\left(2.5,\ 0.8^2\right) = N(2.5,\ 0.64)$, $\quad D \sim N\left(2.0,\ 0.5^2\right) = N(2,\ 0.25)$

Consider $W = X_1 + X_2 - 3D$.

$E(W) = 2.5 + 2.5 - 3(2) = 5 - 6 = -1$

$\operatorname{Var}(W) = 0.64 + 0.64 + 3^2(0.25) = 1.28 + 2.25 = 3.53$

$W \sim N(-1,\ 3.53)$

Required probability $= P\left(X_1 + X_2 > 3D\right) = P(W > 0)$

$= P\left(Z > \dfrac{0 - (-1)}{\sqrt{3.53}}\right) = P(Z > 0.53225)$

$= 0.29727 = 0.297$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: Find the probability that the price of a randomly chosen XO durian differs from the price of a randomly chosen D24 durian by less than \$15. [4]
parts.label: ii

parts.text: A sample of $n$ XO durians is randomly chosen. Find the least value of $n$ such that the probability that the mean mass is more than 2.25 kg exceeds 0.9. [4]
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
For a random sample of $n$ XO durians, the sample mean mass is

$\overline{X} \sim N\left(2.5,\ \dfrac{0.64}{n}\right)$

(exactly normal, since $X$ itself is normally distributed).

We require $P\left(\overline{X} > 2.25\right) > 0.9$.

$P\left(Z > \dfrac{2.25 - 2.5}{0.8/\sqrt{n}}\right) > 0.9$

$P\left(Z > \dfrac{-0.25\sqrt{n}}{0.8}\right) > 0.9$, i.e. $P\left(Z > -0.3125\sqrt{n}\right) > 0.9$

From the standard normal tables, $P(Z > -1.28155) = 0.9$, so we need

$-0.3125\sqrt{n} < -1.28155$

$0.3125\sqrt{n} > 1.28155$

$\sqrt{n} > 4.1010$

$n > 16.818$

$\therefore$ the least value of $n$ is $\mathbf{17}$.

stem:
Six identical boxes are arranged in 3 rows as shown in the following diagram.
Sandra is given 1 green, 2 blue and 3 red balls. The balls are identical except for their colour. She is to put one ball in each box. Find the number of ways she can do this when

parts.text: there is no restriction, [2]
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
There are 6 boxes and 6 balls, one ball per box. The balls consist of 1 green, 2 identical blue and 3 identical red.

The number of distinct arrangements of 6 objects of which 2 are alike of one kind and 3 alike of another is

$\dfrac{6!}{1!\,2!\,3!} = \dfrac{720}{1 \times 2 \times 6} = \dfrac{720}{12} = 60$

There are $60$ ways.

parts.text: the balls in the bottom row are of different colours, [2]
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The bottom row has 3 boxes. For the three balls in it to be of different colours, they must be one green, one blue and one red.

Number of ways to arrange 1 green, 1 blue and 1 red in the 3 bottom boxes $= 3! = 6$

The remaining balls are 1 blue and 2 red, to be placed in the remaining 3 boxes (1 in the top row, 2 in the middle row):

$\dfrac{3!}{1!\,2!} = 3$ ways

Total $= 6 \times 3 = 18$ ways.

parts.text: there are at least 2 red balls in the bottom row. [3]
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
There are 3 red balls altogether and 3 boxes in the bottom row.

$\textbf{Case 1: exactly 2 red balls in the bottom row}$

Choose which 2 of the 3 bottom boxes hold red balls: $\binom{3}{2} = 3$ ways.

The third bottom box holds a green or a blue ball.

$\textit{If it is green}$: the remaining balls are 1 red and 2 blue, placed in the 3 remaining boxes in $\dfrac{3!}{1!\,2!} = 3$ ways.

$\textit{If it is blue}$: the remaining balls are 1 red, 1 blue and 1 green, all different, placed in $3! = 6$ ways.

Case 1 total $= 3 \times (3 + 6) = 3 \times 9 = 27$ ways.

$\textbf{Case 2: all 3 red balls in the bottom row}$

There is $1$ way to fill the bottom row.

The remaining balls are 1 green and 2 blue, placed in the 3 remaining boxes in $\dfrac{3!}{1!\,2!} = 3$ ways.

Case 2 total $= 3$ ways.

Total $= 27 + 3 = 30$ ways.

parts.text:
A special type of jackfruits can be of poor, mediocre and premium grades. The percentage of jackfruits of poor, mediocre and premium grades are on average 20%, 65% and 15% respectively. A customer randomly selects 5 jackfruits. To calculate the probability that 3 of the jackfruits are mediocre and 2 are premium, the following calculation was carried out.
Let $Y$ be the number of mediocre jackfruits
$$Y \sim B(5,\ 0.65)$$
$$P(Y = 3) = {}^{5}C_{3}\,(0.65)^3(1 - 0.65)^2 \approx 0.336$$
Explain, by giving two reasons, why the calculation is not valid. [2]
parts.label: a
parts.answer: Any two of: (1) the event required is not $Y = 3$, since the other 2 jackfruits must specifically be premium, not merely 'not mediocre'; (2) there are more than two outcomes for each jackfruit (poor, mediocre, premium), so a binomial model does not describe the required event; (3) the selections may not be independent / the probability of each grade may not remain constant from one selection to the next, since the jackfruits are selected from a finite stock without replacement.
parts.solution:
$\textbf{Reason 1}$ — The calculation finds $P(Y = 3)$, the probability that exactly 3 of the 5 jackfruits are mediocre. This allows the other 2 jackfruits to be $\textit{either}$ poor $\textit{or}$ premium. The question requires the other 2 to be premium specifically, so $P(Y = 3)$ is not the required probability.

$\textbf{Reason 2}$ — A binomial model requires each trial to have only two outcomes. Here each jackfruit has three possible grades (poor, mediocre, premium), so a single binomial variable cannot describe the joint requirement of 3 mediocre $\textit{and}$ 2 premium.

$\textbf{Reason 3}$ — A binomial model also requires the trials to be independent with a constant probability of success. As the jackfruits are selected from a finite stock without replacement, the probability that a jackfruit is of a given grade changes from selection to selection, so the trials are not independent.

(Any two of the above reasons are required.)

$\textit{For reference}$, the correct probability is
$\dfrac{5!}{3!\,2!}(0.65)^3(0.15)^2 = 10(0.274625)(0.0225) = 0.0618$.

parts.text: A target board in an archery practice school is as shown in the following diagram. The target board is a rectangle with a length of 100 cm and a width of 60 cm. It contains a shaded diamond-shaped region in the middle which has sides of equal lengths.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: By considering the area of the shaded region, show that the probability that an archer will hit the shaded area is 0.15. [1]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
From the diagram, the diamond (a rhombus) has:

horizontal diagonal $= 100 - 20 - 20 = 60$ cm
vertical diagonal $= 60 - 15 - 15 = 30$ cm

Area of a rhombus $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times d_1 \times d_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(60)(30) = 900$ cm$^2$

Area of the rectangular board $= 100 \times 60 = 6000$ cm$^2$

$P(\text{hits shaded area}) = \dfrac{900}{6000} = 0.15$ (shown)

subparts.text: State two assumptions for the probability in part (b)(i) to be valid. [2]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: (1) Every shot the archer takes lands somewhere on the target board; (2) the shot is equally likely to land at any point on the board.
subparts.solution:
$\textbf{Assumption 1}$ — All of the archer's shots hit the target board (no shot misses the board entirely).

$\textbf{Assumption 2}$ — A shot is equally likely to land at any point on the target board, i.e. the landing point is uniformly distributed over the board and the archer does not aim preferentially at the centre.

Only under these assumptions can the probability be taken as the ratio of the areas.

subparts.text: The archer shoots at the target board 100 times as practice. Using a suitable approximation, find the probability that he hits the shaded area more than 20 times. [4]
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Let $X$ be the number of times the archer hits the shaded area out of 100 shots.

$X \sim B(100,\ 0.15)$

Since $n = 100$ is large, $np = 100(0.15) = 15 > 5$ and $nq = 100(0.85) = 85 > 5$, the normal approximation to the binomial is suitable.

$np = 15$, $\quad npq = 100(0.15)(0.85) = 12.75$

$X \sim N(15,\ 12.75)$ approximately

Applying a continuity correction, $P(X > 20) = P(X \geq 21) \to P(Y > 20.5)$:

$P(Y > 20.5) = P\left(Z > \dfrac{20.5 - 15}{\sqrt{12.75}}\right) = P\left(Z > \dfrac{5.5}{3.5707}\right) = P(Z > 1.5403)$

$= 0.06174 = 0.0617$ (3 s.f.)

subparts.text: The archer practised daily for 8 weeks. Each day, he shoots at the target board 100 times. Using a suitable approximation, find the probability that he hits the shaded area at most 9 times in fewer than 4 days. [3]
subparts.label: iv
subparts.solution:
With $X \sim B(100,\ 0.15)$ as before, the probability that on a given day the archer hits the shaded area at most 9 times is, from the GC (exact binomial),

$P(X \leq 9) = 0.055095$

Let $W$ be the number of days, out of $8 \times 7 = 56$ days, on which he hits the shaded area at most 9 times.

$W \sim B(56,\ 0.055095)$

Since $n = 56$ is large ($> 50$) and $np = 56(0.055095) = 3.0853 < 5$, the Poisson approximation to the binomial is suitable.

$W \sim Po(3.0853)$ approximately

$P(W < 4) = P(W \leq 3)$

$= e^{-3.0853}\left(1 + 3.0853 + \dfrac{3.0853^2}{2!} + \dfrac{3.0853^3}{3!}\right)$

$= 0.62813$

$= 0.628$ (3 s.f.)

stem:
Merilian Secondary School has 1600 students. To celebrate its 10th anniversary, the school decides to organise a carnival. A sample of 100 students is to be chosen to take part in a survey. The purpose of the survey is to investigate students' opinions about the types of activities to be included in the carnival.

Describe how the sample could be chosen using systematic sampling. [2]

Give a reason why a stratified sample might be preferable in this context. [2]

Explain whether it would be realistic to use stratified sampling in this context. [1]

Jane and Peter play a game which consists of 2 stages. Each stage is won by either Jane or Peter and the game is won by the player who wins both stages.

The game has the following rules.

**Stage 1**
- A die is tossed once. Jane wins this stage if the score on the die is a '1' or '6'. Otherwise, Peter wins.

**Stage 2**
- The winner of the first stage will draw a card from a deck of 52 playing cards which consists of an equal number of heart, spade, diamond and club suits.
- If the card drawn is not a spade, the player who draws the card wins stage 2. Otherwise, the other player wins.

Construct a probability tree showing this information. [2]

Find the probability that

parts.text: no one wins the game,
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
**Probability tree [2].**
Stage 1: Jane wins with probability $\dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ (score 1 or 6); Peter wins with probability $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
Stage 2: the stage-1 winner draws a card — not a spade with probability $\dfrac{3}{4}$ (that drawer wins stage 2), a spade with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$ (the other player wins stage 2).
The four branches are therefore
$$\text{J, J: } \tfrac{1}{3}\times\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{1}{4}\ (\text{Jane wins the game}); \qquad \text{J, P: } \tfrac{1}{3}\times\tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{12}$$
$$\text{P, P: } \tfrac{2}{3}\times\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}\ (\text{Peter wins the game}); \qquad \text{P, J: } \tfrac{2}{3}\times\tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{6}$$

**(i)** No one wins the game when the two stages are won by different players:
$$P = \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{4}.$$

parts.text: Peter wins the first stage, given that Peter does not win the game.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$P(\text{Peter wins the game}) = \dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $P(\text{Peter does not win the game}) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
$P(\text{Peter wins stage 1} \cap \text{Peter does not win the game}) = \dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{6}$ (the P, J branch).
$$P(\text{Peter wins stage 1} \mid \text{Peter does not win}) = \frac{\frac{1}{6}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{3}.$$

parts.text: The deck of 52 cards is shuffled. 4 cards are drawn at random with replacement. Find the probability that 2 hearts, 1 diamond and 1 spade are drawn.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Drawing with replacement, each card is a heart, diamond, spade or club with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$ each, independently.
The number of orders in which 2 hearts, 1 diamond and 1 spade can appear is
$$\frac{4!}{2!\,1!\,1!} = 12.$$
Each such ordered outcome has probability $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{4} = \dfrac{1}{256}$, so
$$P = 12 \times \frac{1}{256} = \frac{12}{256} = \frac{3}{64}.$$

stem: Ken makes $X$ minutes of outgoing overseas calls and $Y$ minutes of outgoing local calls in a day. $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables. The expected value of $X$ is 2.4 and its standard deviation is 1.5. The expected value of $Y$ is 5 and its standard deviation is 2.5.

parts.text:
Find the probability that, over a 60-day period, the number of minutes of outgoing local calls made by Ken is more than twice the number of minutes of outgoing overseas calls. [4]

Giving a reason, state whether any assumption(s) about the distributions of $X$ and $Y$ are needed for the calculation in part (i) to be valid. [1]
parts.label: i
parts.answer: $0.654$. No assumption is needed: the sample size of 60 is large, so by the Central Limit Theorem the totals are approximately normal.
parts.solution:
Let $S = X_{1} + \cdots + X_{60}$ and $T = Y_{1} + \cdots + Y_{60}$ be the total overseas and local call minutes over the 60 days.
$$E(S) = 60(2.4) = 144, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(S) = 60(1.5)^{2} = 135$$
$$E(T) = 60(5) = 300, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(T) = 60(2.5)^{2} = 375$$
Let $W = T - 2S$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent,
$$E(W) = 300 - 2(144) = 12, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(W) = 375 + 4(135) = 915.$$
Since $n = 60$ is large, by the Central Limit Theorem $S$ and $T$ are approximately normal, hence
$$W \sim \text{N}(12,\ 915) \text{ approximately}, \qquad \sigma_{W} = \sqrt{915} = 30.249.$$
$$P(T > 2S) = P(W > 0) = P\!\left(Z > \frac{0 - 12}{30.249}\right) = P(Z > -0.39670) = 0.65424\ldots = 0.654 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

**Assumption [1].** No assumption about the distributions of $X$ and $Y$ is necessary. The sample size of 60 is large, so by the Central Limit Theorem the totals $S$ and $T$ (and hence $W$) are approximately normally distributed whatever the distributions of $X$ and $Y$.

parts.text:
Outgoing overseas calls cost $\$0.20$ per minute and outgoing local calls cost $\$0.10$ per minute.

Find the probability that, over a 60-day period, the total cost of outgoing calls made by Ken is greater than $\$60$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The total cost over the 60 days is $C = 0.20S + 0.10T$, with $S$ and $T$ as in part (i).
$$E(C) = 0.2(144) + 0.1(300) = 28.8 + 30 = 58.8$$
$$\operatorname{Var}(C) = (0.2)^{2}(135) + (0.1)^{2}(375) = 5.4 + 3.75 = 9.15$$
By the Central Limit Theorem, $C \sim \text{N}(58.8,\ 9.15)$ approximately, with $\sigma_{C} = \sqrt{9.15} = 3.0249$.
$$P(C > 60) = P\!\left(Z > \frac{60 - 58.8}{3.0249}\right) = P(Z > 0.39670) = 0.34576\ldots = 0.346 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

parts.text:
The number of incoming calls received by Ken in a day is a random variable with the distribution Po(3).

Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that, over a 60-day period, the number of incoming calls received by Ken is at most 200.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Let $N$ be the number of incoming calls over the 60 days. Since the daily numbers are independent Po(3) variables,
$$N \sim \text{Po}(60 \times 3) = \text{Po}(180).$$
As $\lambda = 180 > 10$, use the normal approximation
$$N \sim \text{N}(180,\ 180) \text{ approximately}, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{180} = 13.416.$$
Applying a continuity correction,
$$P(N \leq 200) \approx P(N_{\text{normal}} < 200.5) = P\!\left(Z < \frac{200.5 - 180}{13.416}\right) = P(Z < 1.52798) = 0.93672\ldots$$
$$P(N \leq 200) = 0.937 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$
(Without the continuity correction the value is $0.932$.)

stem: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left( 2r + 1 + \frac{1}{r(r+1)} \right) = (n+1)^2 - \frac{1}{n+1}$. [5] Hence find the least $n$ such that $$\sum_{r=10}^{n}\left( 2r + 1 + \frac{1}{r(r+1)} \right) > 525$$ [3]

Sketch on an Argand diagram the set of points representing all complex numbers $z$ satisfying all of the following inequalities: [4] $$\left\lvert z + 1 + i \right\rvert \leq \sqrt{2}, \quad \left\lvert z + 1 + i \right\rvert \geq \left\lvert z - 1 + i \right\rvert \quad \text{and} \quad -\frac{\pi}{4} \leq \arg(z + 1 + i) < \frac{\pi}{4}$$ Hence find

parts.text: the least possible exact value of $\left\lvert z - 3 - 2i \right\rvert$,
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
[The sketch answering the stem is shown in the diagram.]
$\left\lvert z + 1 + i \right\rvert \leq \sqrt{2}$ is the closed disc centred at $A(-1,\ -1)$ of radius $\sqrt{2}$.
$\left\lvert z - (-1 - i) \right\rvert \geq \left\lvert z - (1 - i) \right\rvert$ is the set of points at least as close to $(1,\ -1)$ as to $(-1,\ -1)$, i.e. the half-plane $x \geq 0$ (right of the perpendicular bisector of the two points).
$-\frac{\pi}{4} \leq \arg\left( z - (-1 - i) \right) < \frac{\pi}{4}$ is the sector at $A$ between the half-lines at $-\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
The two arc ends of that sector are $A + \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{cis}\left(\pm\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = (0,\ 0)$ and $(0,\ -2)$, so the region is the circular segment bounded by the arc and the segment of the line $x = 0$ from $(0,\ -2)$ to $(0,\ 0)$.

$\left\lvert z - (3 + 2i) \right\rvert$ is the distance from $B(3,\ 2)$ to a point of the region.
$AB = \sqrt{(3+1)^2 + (2+1)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$.
The nearest point of the disc to $B$ lies on $AB$ at distance $AB - \sqrt{2}$ from $B$; that point is $A + \sqrt{2}\left( \frac{4}{5},\ \frac{3}{5} \right) = (0.131,\ -0.151)$, which lies in the region (it has $x \geq 0$ and $\arg = \tan^{-1}\frac{3}{4} = 0.6435 < \frac{\pi}{4}$).
Hence the least value of $\left\lvert z - 3 - 2i \right\rvert = 5 - \sqrt{2}$.

parts.text: the largest possible value of $\arg(z - 3 - 2i)$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Every point of the region lies below and to the left of $B(3,\ 2)$, so $\arg\left( z - (3+2i) \right)$ is a third-quadrant angle in $\left( -\pi,\ -\frac{\pi}{2} \right)$; the largest such argument is obtained at the point where the line from $B$ touches the circle on the upper side.
$\arg\left( A - B \right) = \arg(-4 - 3i) = -\left( \pi - \tan^{-1}\frac{3}{4} \right) = -2.4981$ rad.
The tangent from $B$ makes an angle $\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5} = 0.28687$ rad with $BA$.
Largest $\arg(z - 3 - 2i) = -2.4981 + 0.28687 = -2.2112 = -2.21$ rad (3 s.f.).
(The tangency point lies on the arc within the sector, so it belongs to the region; the corner $z = -2i$ gives the marginally smaller $-2.2143$ rad.)

stem:
Referred to an origin $O$, the position vectors of two points $A$ and $B$ are $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ respectively. State the geometrical interpretation of $\left|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\right|$. [1]

Given that $\left|\mathbf{a}\right| = 2$ and $\left|\mathbf{b}\right| = 3$, find the value of $\left(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}\right)$. [2]

Given further that the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, find the exact value of $\left|\left(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}\right) \times \left(\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}\right)\right|$. [4]

A website "Koogle" receives hits at a rate of 120 per hour. State two conditions required for the number of hits obtained in a 1-minute interval to be well modelled by a Poisson distribution. [2]

Assume that the number of hits "Koogle" receives in a 1-minute interval follows a Poisson distribution.

parts.text: Find the probability that in a 2-minute interval, the number of hits received by "Koogle" is less than 5.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
**Stem: conditions for a Poisson model.**

1. The hits occur independently of one another (and singly, at random, in the interval).
2. The mean number of hits in a 1-minute interval is constant, i.e. hits occur at a constant average rate over time.

**(i)**

"Koogle" receives $120$ hits per hour, i.e. $\dfrac{120}{60} = 2$ hits per minute.

Let $K$ be the number of hits in a 2-minute interval, so $K \sim \mathrm{Po}(4)$.

$$P(K < 5) = P(K \le 4) = 0.62884\ldots \approx 0.629$$

parts.text: Another website "Noogle" receives hits at a rate of 360 per hour. The number of hits it receives in a 1-minute interval is an independent random variable that follows a Poisson distribution. Find the probability that in a 1-minute interval, the total number of hits received by both websites is more than 10.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
"Noogle" receives $\dfrac{360}{60} = 6$ hits per minute.

In a 1-minute interval, let $K_1 \sim \mathrm{Po}(2)$ and $N_1 \sim \mathrm{Po}(6)$ be the hits received by "Koogle" and "Noogle" respectively. Since they are independent, the sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson:

$$T = K_1 + N_1 \sim \mathrm{Po}\left(2 + 6\right) = \mathrm{Po}(8)$$

$$P(T > 10) = 1 - P(T \le 10) = 1 - 0.81589 = 0.18411\ldots$$

$$\approx 0.184$$

parts.text: By using suitable approximations, find the probability that in a 30-minute interval, the number of hits received by "Noogle" is at least 4 times as many as that received by "Koogle".
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
In a 30-minute interval, let $K$ and $N$ be the numbers of hits received by "Koogle" and "Noogle" respectively:
$$K \sim \mathrm{Po}\left(30 \times 2\right) = \mathrm{Po}(60), \qquad N \sim \mathrm{Po}\left(30 \times 6\right) = \mathrm{Po}(180).$$

Since $\lambda = 60 > 10$ and $\lambda = 180 > 10$, both may be approximated by normal distributions:
$$K \sim \mathrm{N}\left(60,\ 60\right) \text{ approximately}, \qquad N \sim \mathrm{N}\left(180,\ 180\right) \text{ approximately}.$$

We require $P\left(N \ge 4K\right) = P\left(N - 4K \ge 0\right)$.

Since $K$ and $N$ are independent,
$$E\left(N - 4K\right) = 180 - 4(60) = -60$$
$$\mathrm{Var}\left(N - 4K\right) = 180 + 4^2(60) = 180 + 960 = 1140$$
$$N - 4K \sim \mathrm{N}\left(-60,\ 1140\right) \text{ approximately}.$$

Applying a continuity correction (since $N - 4K$ takes integer values):
$$P\left(N - 4K \ge 0\right) \approx P\left(N - 4K > -0.5\right)$$

$$z = \frac{-0.5 - \left(-60\right)}{\sqrt{1140}} = \frac{59.5}{33.7639} = 1.76222$$

$$P\left(Z > 1.76222\right) = 0.039028\ldots \approx 0.0390$$

stem: Find the expansion of $\left(\dfrac{1 + 2x^2}{4 - x}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^2$. [4]

parts.text: Find the set of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
**The expansion (stem).**

$$\left(\frac{1 + 2x^2}{4 - x}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \left(1 + 2x^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(4 - x\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$$

$$\left(1 + 2x^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}\left(2x^2\right) + \ldots = 1 + x^2 + \ldots$$

$$\left(4 - x\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 4^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(1 - \frac{x}{4}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{x}{4}\right) + \frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)}{2!}\left(-\frac{x}{4}\right)^2 + \ldots\right]$$
$$= \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{x}{8} + \frac{3}{8}\cdot\frac{x^2}{16} + \ldots\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{x}{8} + \frac{3x^2}{128} + \ldots\right)$$

Multiplying and keeping terms up to $x^2$:
$$\left(1 + x^2\right)\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{x}{8} + \frac{3x^2}{128}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{8}x + \left(\frac{3}{128} + 1\right)x^2 + \ldots\right)$$
$$= \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{8}x + \frac{131}{128}x^2\right) + \ldots$$

**(i) Validity.**

$\left(1 + 2x^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is valid for $\left|2x^2\right| < 1$, i.e. $\left|x\right| < \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

$\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{4}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ is valid for $\left|\dfrac{x}{4}\right| < 1$, i.e. $\left|x\right| < 4$.

Both must hold, so the expansion is valid for
$$-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < x < \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \qquad \text{i.e. } \left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < x < \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right\}.$$

parts.text: By putting $x = \dfrac{1}{4}$, show that $\sqrt{30} \approx \dfrac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers to be determined.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Note $x = \dfrac{1}{4}$ lies in the valid interval, since $\dfrac{1}{4} < \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Left-hand side:
$$\left(\frac{1 + 2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2}{4 - \frac{1}{4}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \left(\frac{1 + \frac{1}{8}}{\frac{15}{4}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \left(\frac{\frac{9}{8}}{\frac{15}{4}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \left(\frac{3}{10}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{10}}$$

Right-hand side:
$$\frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{1}{4} + \frac{131}{128}\cdot\frac{1}{16}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{32} + \frac{131}{2048}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2048 + 64 + 131}{2048} = \frac{2243}{4096}$$

So $\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{10}} \approx \dfrac{2243}{4096}$. Taking reciprocals,
$$\sqrt{\frac{10}{3}} \approx \frac{4096}{2243}, \qquad \text{and } \sqrt{\frac{10}{3}} = \frac{\sqrt{30}}{3},$$

so
$$\sqrt{30} \approx 3 \times \frac{4096}{2243} = \frac{12288}{2243},$$

i.e. $a = 12288$ and $b = 2243$. (This gives $5.4784$, against the true value $\sqrt{30} = 5.4772$.)

*Note:* working directly instead, $\sqrt{30} = 10\sqrt{\frac{3}{10}} \approx \dfrac{22430}{4096} = \dfrac{11215}{2048}$, which is equally acceptable; the mark scheme quotes the reciprocal form above.

stem:
The plane $p_1$ has equation $2x - 3y + z = 8$ and it meets the $x$- and $z$-axes at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. State the position vectors of $A$ and $B$, relative to the origin, and show that a cartesian equation of the line $AB$ is $4 - x = \dfrac{z}{2}$, $y = 0$. [4]

The point $C$ lies on $AB$ such that $\dfrac{AC}{CB} = \dfrac{1}{3}$. The plane $p_2$ passes through $C$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}$. Given that $p_2$ is also perpendicular to $p_1$, find

parts.text: the cartesian equation of $p_2$;
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
**Stem.**

$A$ is on the $x$-axis, so $y = z = 0$: $2x = 8 \implies x = 4$, giving $\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

$B$ is on the $z$-axis, so $x = y = 0$: $z = 8$, giving $\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$.

$$\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 0 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} = 4\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$$

Line $AB$: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, so $x = 4 - \lambda$, $y = 0$, $z = 2\lambda$.

From these, $\lambda = 4 - x$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{z}{2}$, so
$$4 - x = \frac{z}{2}, \qquad y = 0$$
as required.

**(i) Equation of $p_2$.**

$\dfrac{AC}{CB} = \dfrac{1}{3}$, so $C$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $1 : 3$ and by the ratio theorem
$$\overrightarrow{OC} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \frac{1}{4}\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 0 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}.$$

$p_2$ is parallel to $\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Since $p_2 \perp p_1$, the normal of $p_1$, $\mathbf{n}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, is parallel to $p_2$. So a normal to $p_2$ is

$$\mathbf{n}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} (-2)(1) - (0)(-3) \\ (0)(2) - (1)(1) \\ (1)(-3) - (-2)(2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Taking $\mathbf{n}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and using $C(3,\ 0,\ 2)$:
$$\mathbf{n}_2 \cdot \overrightarrow{OC} = 2(3) + 1(0) - 1(2) = 4$$

$$p_2 : 2x + y - z = 4$$

parts.text: the perpendicular distance from $A$ to $p_2$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$$\text{Distance} = \frac{\left|\mathbf{n}_2\cdot\overrightarrow{OA} - 4\right|}{\left|\mathbf{n}_2\right|} = \frac{\left|2(4) + 1(0) - 1(0) - 4\right|}{\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2 + (-1)^2}} = \frac{\left|8 - 4\right|}{\sqrt{6}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}$$

$$= \frac{4\sqrt{6}}{6} = \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3} \approx 1.63 \text{ units}$$

stem: The number of flaws in a roll of microfleece fabric is known to follow a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$. A roll of microfleece fabric is chosen at random. Given that the probability that it contains no flaws is 0.9, find the value of $\lambda$, correct to 4 decimal places. [2] A random sample of $n$ rolls of microfleece fabric is taken.

parts.text: If $n = 80$, find the probability that the mean number of flaws per roll is less than 0.1.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let $X$ be the number of flaws in a roll, $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$.
$P(X = 0) = e^{-\lambda} = 0.9 \Rightarrow \lambda = -\ln 0.9 = 0.105361 = 0.1054$ (4 d.p.).

For $n = 80$ rolls, $E(X) = \lambda$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = \lambda$, so since $n = 80$ is large, by the Central Limit Theorem
$\overline{X} \sim N\left( 0.105361,\ \frac{0.105361}{80} \right) = N\left( 0.105361,\ 0.00131701 \right)$ approximately.
$P\left( \overline{X} < 0.1 \right) = P\left( Z < \frac{0.1 - 0.105361}{0.0362905} \right) = P(Z < -0.14772) = 0.441$ (3 s.f.).

parts.text: The probability that there is at most 1 roll containing no flaws is less than 0.02.
parts.label: b

subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let $Y$ be the number of the $n$ rolls that contain no flaws. Each roll independently contains no flaws with probability 0.9, so $Y \sim B(n,\ 0.9)$.
$P(Y \leq 1) = P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1) = (0.1)^n + \binom{n}{1}(0.9)(0.1)^{n-1}$
$= (0.1)^n + 9n(0.1)^n$, since $n(0.9)(0.1)^{n-1} = 9n(0.1)^{n}$
$= (0.1)^n(1 + 9n)$.
Requiring this to be less than 0.02 gives $(0.1)^n(1 + 9n) < 0.02$ (shown).

subparts.text: Hence find the least value of $n$.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Tabulating $f(n) = (0.1)^n(1 + 9n)$:
$f(1) = 1$, $f(2) = 0.19$, $f(3) = 0.028$, $f(4) = 0.0037$.
$f(n)$ decreases as $n$ increases, and $f(3) = 0.028 > 0.02$ while $f(4) = 0.0037 < 0.02$.
Hence the least value of $n$ is 4.

stem: The diagram above shows the graph of $C_{1}$ with equation $\frac{(x-a)^{2}}{b^{2}} - (y-c)^{2} = 1$ where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive constants. The lines $y = \frac{x}{2}$ and $y = -\frac{x}{2}+2$ are asymptotes of $C_{1}$. Given that one of the vertices of $C_{1}$ lies on the $y$-axis, find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] The curve $C_{2}$ has equation $(x-1)^{2} + k(y-1)^{2} = k$ where $k$ is a positive constant. Find the range of values of $k$ such that $C_{2}$ intersects $C_{1}$ at exactly 4 distinct points. [3]

A curve $C$ has equation $y^2 = 4x$ and a line $l$ has equation $2x - y + 1 = 0$. The diagram above shows the graphs of $C$ and $l$.

$B\left(b,\ 2\sqrt{b}\right)$ is a fixed point on $C$ and $A$ is an arbitrary point on $l$. State the geometrical relationship between the line segment $AB$ and $l$ if the distance from $B$ to $A$ is the least. [1]

Taking the coordinates of $A$ as $(a,\ 2a + 1)$, find an equation relating $a$ and $b$ for which $AB$ is the least. [2]

Deduce that when $AB$ is the least, $(AB)^2 = m\left(2b - 2\sqrt{b} + 1\right)^2$, where $m$ is a constant to be found.

Hence or otherwise, find the coordinates of the point on $C$ that is nearest to $l$, as $b$ varies. [5]

The numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are represented on the number line. Match the values below to the numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [2]
$$\dfrac{4}{5},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ 0.3,\ \dfrac{5}{4}$$

Based on past records, there is a probability of $p$ that a customer with a hotel reservation will not show up. State two assumptions needed such that the number of customers who do not show up at the hotel may be well modelled by a Binomial Distribution. [2]
Assume now that these assumptions do in fact hold.
Hotel TM has a capacity of 200 rooms. In order to maximize profits, Hotel TM will accept more reservations than their capacity. The hotel is overbooked if there are not enough rooms available for customers who show up on that day.

parts.text: Given that $p = 0.08$, find the probability that Hotel TM is not overbooked when 220 reservations are accepted for the day.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Let $X$ be the number of the 220 customers who do not show up, so $X \sim B(220,\ 0.08)$.
The number who show up is $220 - X$, and the hotel is not overbooked when $220 - X \leq 200$, i.e. $X \geq 20$.
$$P(X \geq 20) = 1 - P(X \leq 19) = 1 - 0.69113 = 0.30887 = 0.309 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

parts.text: The probability that Hotel TM is overbooked when 210 reservations are accepted is 0.12. Find the value of $p$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Let $Y$ be the number of the 210 customers who do not show up, so $Y \sim B(210,\ p)$.
The hotel is overbooked when $210 - Y > 200$, i.e. $Y \leq 9$.
$$P(Y \leq 9) = 0.12$$
Solving with a graphing calculator gives $p = 0.0649$ (3 s.f.).

parts.text: Use the substitution $u = 1 - x^{2}$ to find $\int 2x^{3}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\,dx$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
With $u = 1 - x^{2}$, $du = -2x\,dx$ and $x^{2} = 1 - u$:
$\int 2x^{3}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\,dx = \int x^{2}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\,(2x\,dx) = -\int (1 - u)\sqrt{u}\,du$
$= \int \left(u\sqrt{u} - \sqrt{u}\right)du$
$= \frac{2}{5}u^{\frac{5}{2}} - \frac{2}{3}u^{\frac{3}{2}} + C$
$= \frac{2}{5}\left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}} - \frac{2}{3}\left(1 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C$

parts.text: Find $\int \frac{x - 1}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx$. [2] Hence find $\int \frac{x - 4}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx$. [3]
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$\int \frac{x - 1}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx = \frac{1}{4}\int \frac{4x - 4}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx = \frac{1}{4}\ln\lvert 2x^{2} - 4x + 1 \rvert + C$
For the second integral, write $x - 4 = (x - 1) - 3$:
$\int \frac{x - 4}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx = \int \frac{x - 1}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx - \int \frac{3}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx$
$2x^{2} - 4x + 1 = 2\left[(x - 1)^{2} - \frac{1}{2}\right]$, so
$\int \frac{3}{2x^{2} - 4x + 1}\,dx = \frac{3}{2}\int \frac{dx}{(x - 1)^{2} - \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}} = \frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}\ln\left\lvert \frac{x - 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{x - 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \right\rvert + C$
$= \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\ln\left\lvert \frac{\sqrt{2}x - \sqrt{2} - 1}{\sqrt{2}x - \sqrt{2} + 1} \right\rvert + C$
Hence the integral is $\frac{1}{4}\ln\lvert 2x^{2} - 4x + 1 \rvert - \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\ln\left\lvert \frac{\sqrt{2}x - \sqrt{2} - 1}{\sqrt{2}x - \sqrt{2} + 1} \right\rvert + C$

stem: The plane $\pi$ has equation $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 12 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \beta\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix},\ \alpha,\ \beta \in \mathbb{R}$.

parts.text: The point $A$ has coordinates $(1,\ 2,\ 3)$. The point $B$, the reflection of $A$ in $\pi$, has coordinates $(-5,\ c,\ -9)$. By considering the mid-point of $AB$, or otherwise, find the value of $c$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
A normal to $\pi$ is
$\mathbf{n} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$
Since $B$ is the reflection of $A$ in $\pi$, the mid-point $M$ of $AB$ lies on $\pi$:
$M = \left(\frac{1 + (-5)}{2},\ \frac{2 + c}{2},\ \frac{3 + (-9)}{2}\right) = \left(-2,\ \frac{2 + c}{2},\ -3\right)$
$M$ lies on $\pi$, so $\left(\overrightarrow{OM} - \begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 12 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}\right)\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ \frac{c - 22}{2} \\ -7 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} = 0$
$-6 + (c - 22) + 14 = 0$
$c = 14$

parts.text: The line $l$ is parallel to $\pi$ and has equation $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix},\ \lambda \in \mathbb{R}$. Find the distance between $l$ and $\pi$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Since $l$ is parallel to $\pi$, the distance between them is the distance from any point of $l$ to $\pi$. Take the point $(4,\ 0,\ -8)$ on $l$ and the point $(-8,\ 12,\ 4)$ on $\pi$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 12 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ -12 \\ -12 \end{pmatrix}$
With $\mathbf{n} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\lvert \mathbf{n} \rvert = 3$:
Distance $= \left\lvert \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ -12 \\ -12 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} \right\rvert = \left\lvert \frac{-12 - 24 + 24}{3} \right\rvert = 4$
The distance between $l$ and $\pi$ is 4 units.

parts.text: The variable point $P$ moves along $l$ and the variable point $Q$ moves on $\pi$. The point $R$ lies on the line segment $PQ$ such that $PR = 3RQ$. Find $\overrightarrow{OR}$ in terms of $\alpha,\ \beta$ and $\lambda$. [2] Hence give a geometrical description of the locus of $R$. [2]
parts.label: iii
parts.answer: $\overrightarrow{OR} = \begin{pmatrix} -5 \\ 9 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \left(\frac{3}{4}\alpha + \frac{1}{4}\lambda\right)\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{3}{4}\beta\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$; the locus of $R$ is a plane parallel to $\pi$, lying between $l$ and $\pi$ at a distance of 1 unit from $\pi$ (3 units from $l$).
parts.solution:
$PR = 3RQ$ and $R$ lies on $PQ$, so $\overrightarrow{PR} = \frac{3}{4}\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and
$\overrightarrow{OR} = \frac{1}{4}\overrightarrow{OP} + \frac{3}{4}\overrightarrow{OQ}$
$= \frac{1}{4}\left[\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right] + \frac{3}{4}\left[\begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 12 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \beta\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\right]$
$= \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 9 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \left(\frac{1}{4}\lambda + \frac{3}{4}\alpha\right)\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{3}{4}\beta\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$
$= \begin{pmatrix} -5 \\ 9 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \left(\frac{3}{4}\alpha + \frac{1}{4}\lambda\right)\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{3}{4}\beta\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$
As $\alpha,\ \beta,\ \lambda$ vary over $\mathbb{R}$, the two coefficients take every real value independently, so $R$ traces the whole plane through $(-5,\ 9,\ 1)$ with direction vectors $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ — a plane parallel to $\pi$.
Its distance from $\pi$ is
$\left\lvert \frac{1}{3}\left[\begin{pmatrix} -5 \\ 9 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 12 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}\right]\cdot\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} \right\rvert = \left\lvert \frac{-3 - 6 + 6}{3} \right\rvert = 1$
So the locus of $R$ is the plane parallel to $\pi$ that lies between $\pi$ and $l$, 1 unit from $\pi$ and 3 units from $l$.

stem: Two groups of researchers are investigating the spread of a virus in a city. $x$ people are infected $t$ weeks after the virus is first discovered.

parts.text: In the absence of vaccination, the first group of researchers suspected that $x$ and $t$ are related by the differential equation $\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} = \frac{t}{\left(1 + t^{2}\right)^{2}}$. Initially, 20 people are infected with the virus and one week later 30 people are infected with the virus. Find $x$ in terms of $t$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Integrate once with respect to $t$:
$\frac{dx}{dt} = \int \frac{t}{\left(1 + t^{2}\right)^{2}}\,dt = \frac{1}{2}\int \left(1 + t^{2}\right)^{-2}(2t)\,dt = -\frac{1}{2\left(1 + t^{2}\right)} + A$
Integrate again:
$x = -\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} t + At + B$
Initially $t = 0$, $x = 20$: $B = 20$.
When $t = 1$, $x = 30$:
$30 = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + A + 20$
$A = 10 + \frac{\pi}{8}$
$x = -\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} t + \left(10 + \frac{\pi}{8}\right)t + 20$

parts.text: The second group of researchers suspected that the population of infected people increases at a constant rate of $r$ people per week. A vaccine believed to be able to reduce the population of infected people at a rate proportional to the number of infected people was introduced when the virus started to spread. Initially $a$ people are infected with the virus. The population of infected people is found to remain constant at the instant when it reaches $2a$. Show that a differential equation satisfied by $x$ and $t$ is of the form $\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{r}{2a}(2a - x)$. [2] Find $x$ in terms of $a$, $r$ and $t$. [4]
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The population increases at a constant rate $r$ and decreases at a rate proportional to $x$:
$\frac{dx}{dt} = r - kx$ for some constant $k > 0$.
The population is constant when $x = 2a$, so $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ there:
$r - 2ak = 0 \Rightarrow k = \frac{r}{2a}$
$\frac{dx}{dt} = r - \frac{r}{2a}x = \frac{r}{2a}(2a - x)$ (shown)
Separating the variables:
$\int \frac{1}{2a - x}\,dx = \int \frac{r}{2a}\,dt$
$-\ln\lvert 2a - x \rvert = \frac{r}{2a}t + c$
$2a - x = Ce^{-\frac{r}{2a}t}$
Initially $t = 0$, $x = a$: $2a - a = C$, so $C = a$.
$x = 2a - ae^{-\frac{r}{2a}t}$

stem:
Without using a calculator, solve the inequality $ rac{x}{2x - 1} \leq  rac{3}{x + 1}$, where $x 
eq  rac{1}{2}$ and $x 
eq -1$. [4] Hence find the exact solution of the inequality $ rac{x}{2x + 1} \leq  rac{3}{1 - x}$, where $x 
eq 1$ and $x 
eq - rac{1}{2}$. [2]

A property developer decides to divide a triangular plot of land $PQR$ into two plots of equal area. One section, $MNP$, is to be used for commercial development and the other, $MNQR$, is to be used for high-rise residential development. It is given that $PN = x$ km, $PM = y$ km, $MN = z$ km, $PR = 1.2$ km, $PQ = 1.4$ km, and $\angle QPR = \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is a constant. Show that $z^{2} = x^{2} + \frac{0.7056}{x^{2}} - 1.68\cos\alpha$. [3] To minimize construction costs, the architects have decided that the boundary $MN$ should preferably be of the minimum possible length. Using differentiation, find the value of $x$ which will minimise the construction cost. [5]

At a medieval-themed carnival, a replica ballista (a powerful historical siege weapon designed to shoot large spears in straight lines) is set up to entertain the visitors. The ballista is designed to shoot horizontally, and also up to $\frac{\pi}{6}$ radians above the horizontal. A vertical target board is set up 30 m from the ballista, and the height of the target board is initially measured to match the trajectory of the ballista's missiles. As a safety precaution, the target board is extended by $d$ m to account for an extra $\theta$ radians of elevation beyond the initial limit. Given that $\theta$ is small, show that $d \approx 30\left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}\theta}{\sqrt{3} - \theta} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$. [5] Hence, express $d$ as a polynomial in $\theta$, up to and including the term in $\theta^{2}$. [3]
The figure below shows part of the track of a roller-coaster which is modelled by a curve with the parametric equations $x = 2\theta - \sin\theta,\ y = 4\cos\theta$, for $0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi$.

parts.text: Find the exact coordinates of the lowest point on the track.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = 2 - \cos\theta$ and $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -4\sin\theta$, so
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-4\sin\theta}{2 - \cos\theta}$
Since $2 - \cos\theta > 0$ for all $\theta$, $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ when $\sin\theta = 0$, i.e. $\theta = 0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$ in the given range.
$y = 4\cos\theta$ is least when $\cos\theta = -1$, i.e. $\theta = \pi$:
$x = 2\pi - \sin\pi = 2\pi$, $y = 4\cos\pi = -4$
The lowest point is $(2\pi,\ -4)$.

parts.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at point $A$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$A$ is the point where the curve first meets the $x$-axis, so $4\cos\theta = 0$ with $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$:
$x = 2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - \sin\frac{\pi}{2} = \pi - 1$, $y = 0$, so $A(\pi - 1,\ 0)$.
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-4\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}{2 - \cos\frac{\pi}{2}} = \frac{-4}{2} = -2$
Equation of the tangent at $A$:
$y - 0 = -2\left(x - (\pi - 1)\right)$
$y = -2x + 2\pi - 2$

parts.text: Show that the area of the region bounded by the curve and the $x$-axis is given by $\int_{a}^{b}\left(8\cos\theta - 4\cos^{2}\theta\right)d\theta$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants to be determined. [2] Hence find the exact area of this region. [3]
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
The curve meets the $x$-axis where $4\cos\theta = 0$, i.e. $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$; between these the curve lies below the $x$-axis.
With $dx = (2 - \cos\theta)\,d\theta$,
$y\,dx = 4\cos\theta\,(2 - \cos\theta)\,d\theta = \left(8\cos\theta - 4\cos^{2}\theta\right)d\theta$
Because the region lies below the axis, the area is the integral taken from $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ to $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$, so $a = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ and $b = \frac{\pi}{2}$.
Using $\cos^{2}\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}$:
$\int \left(8\cos\theta - 4\cos^{2}\theta\right)d\theta = 8\sin\theta - 2\theta - \sin 2\theta + c$
Evaluating from $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ to $\frac{\pi}{2}$:
At $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$: $8(1) - \pi - 0 = 8 - \pi$
At $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$: $8(-1) - 3\pi - 0 = -8 - 3\pi$
Area $= (8 - \pi) - (-8 - 3\pi) = 16 + 2\pi$

stem: The figure below shows a solid cylindrical micro-filtration device with height 4 cm, base radius 2 cm and a hollow section for inserting disposable micro-filters. The hollow section is formed by rotating part of the curve $y = 2^{x^{2}} + A$, where $A$ is a constant, about the $y$-axis. The origin $O$ is taken to be the centre of the circular base. Given that the lowest point of the hollow section is 3 cm vertically above $O$, write down the value of $A$. [1] Hence show that the volume of material required to fabricate the device is $\left(14 + \frac{1}{\ln 2}\right)\pi$ cm$^{3}$. [6]

The functions $f$ and $g$ are given by
$$f: x \mapsto x^{2} - 4x + 1 \quad \text{for } x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \leq k$$
$$g: x \mapsto \ln(1 + x) \quad \text{for } x \in \mathbb{R},\ x > -1$$
Find the largest value of $k$, given that $f^{-1}$ exists, and express $f^{-1}$ in a similar form. [4]

parts.text: Explain why $fg$ does not exist.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
(Stem) $f(x) = x^{2}-4x+1 = (x-2)^{2}-3$, a parabola with line of symmetry $x=2$.
$f$ is one-one on $x \leq k$ only when $k \leq 2$, so the largest value is $k = 2$.
Let $y = (x-2)^{2}-3$. Then $(x-2)^{2} = y+3$ and, since $x \leq 2$, $x = 2-\sqrt{y+3}$.
$R_{f} = [-3, \infty)$, so $f^{-1}: x \mapsto 2-\sqrt{x+3}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \geq -3$.
(i) $R_{g} = (-\infty, \infty)$ while $D_{f} = (-\infty, 2]$.
Since $R_{g} \not\subseteq D_{f}$, the composite $fg$ does not exist.

parts.text: Given that $g_{1}$ is a restricted function of $g$ such that $fg_{1}$ is a function, find the largest possible domain of $g_{1}$, giving your answer in exact form. Hence express $fg_{1}$ in a similar form and state its range.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$fg_{1}$ exists $\iff R_{g_{1}} \subseteq D_{f} = (-\infty, 2]$, i.e. $\ln(1+x) \leq 2$.
So $1+x \leq e^{2}$, giving $x \leq e^{2}-1$; together with $x > -1$ from $g$,
the largest domain is $D_{g_{1}} = \left(-1,\ e^{2}-1\right]$.
$fg_{1}(x) = f\!\left(\ln(1+x)\right) = \left[\ln(1+x)\right]^{2} - 4\ln(1+x) + 1$,
so $fg_{1}: x \mapsto \left[\ln(1+x)\right]^{2} - 4\ln(1+x) + 1$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $-1 < x \leq e^{2}-1$.
With $u = \ln(1+x)$, $u$ runs over $(-\infty, 2]$ and $f(u) = (u-2)^{2}-3$ decreases to a minimum of $-3$ at $u=2$,
so $R_{fg_{1}} = [-3, \infty)$.

stem:
Prove by induction that
$$\sum_{r = 1}^{n}(r + 1)^{2}\,r! = (n + 2)! - 2.$$
[5]

parts.label: i
parts.solution:
(Stem) Let $P_{n}$ be the statement $\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r+1)^{2}r! = (n+2)!-2$.
$P_{1}$: LHS $= (2)^{2}(1!) = 4$; RHS $= 3!-2 = 4$. So $P_{1}$ is true.
Assume $P_{k}$ true for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$: $\sum_{r=1}^{k}(r+1)^{2}r! = (k+2)!-2$.
Then $\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}(r+1)^{2}r! = (k+2)!-2 + (k+2)^{2}(k+1)!$
$= (k+2)(k+1)! - 2 + (k+2)^{2}(k+1)! = (k+1)!\,(k+2)\left[1 + (k+2)\right] - 2$
$= (k+2)!\,(k+3) - 2 = (k+3)!-2$, which is $P_{k+1}$.
Since $P_{1}$ is true and $P_{k}$ true $\Rightarrow P_{k+1}$ true, $P_{n}$ is true for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$.
(i) The given sum is $\sum_{r=2}^{n}(r+1)^{2}r!$, i.e. the proved sum with the $r=1$ term removed:
$$(n+2)! - 2 - (2)^{2}(1!) = (n+2)! - 6.$$

parts.text: Using the method of differences, find $\sum_{r = 1}^{n}\left[(r + 1)! - r!\right]$ in terms of $n$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+1)!-r!\right] = (2!-1!)+(3!-2!)+\ldots+\left[(n+1)!-n!\right] = (n+1)!-1!,$$
so the sum is $(n+1)!-1$.

parts.text: By considering $(r + 1)^{2}r! + \left[(r + 1)! - r!\right]$, deduce $\sum_{r = 1}^{n}\left(r^{2} + 3r + 1\right)r!$ in terms of $n$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
$(r+1)^{2}r! + \left[(r+1)!-r!\right] = (r^{2}+2r+1)r! + (r+1)r! - r!$
$= \left[(r^{2}+2r+1) + (r+1) - 1\right]r! = (r^{2}+3r+1)r!$.
Summing from $r=1$ to $n$ and using the two results above:
$$\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r^{2}+3r+1)r! = \left[(n+2)!-2\right] + \left[(n+1)!-1\right] = (n+2)!+(n+1)!-3.$$
This may be written $(n+1)!\left[(n+2)+1\right]-3 = (n+1)!(n+3)-3$.

stem:
Given that $y = \sqrt{3 + \sin^{2}x}$, show that
(i) $2y\frac{dy}{dx} = \sin 2x$,
(ii) $y\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2} = \cos 2x$. [3]
Find the Maclaurin series of $y$, up to and including the term in $x^{4}$. [5]
By substituting $x = \frac{\pi}{3}$, show that $\sqrt{15} \approx 2\sqrt{3}\left(1 + \frac{\pi^{2}}{54} - \frac{5\pi^{4}}{5832}\right)$. [2]

subparts.text: Find the fifth roots of $-243$, expressing the roots in the form $re^{i\theta}$, where $r > 0$ and $-\pi < \theta \leq \pi$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$-243 = 243e^{i(\pi + 2k\pi)}$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Taking fifth roots: $z = 243^{1/5}e^{i\left(\frac{\pi + 2k\pi}{5}\right)} = 3e^{i\left(\frac{\pi+2k\pi}{5}\right)}$.
Choosing $k = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2$ keeps $\theta \in (-\pi, \pi]$:
$3e^{i\frac{\pi}{5}},\ 3e^{i\frac{3\pi}{5}},\ 3e^{i\pi},\ 3e^{-i\frac{\pi}{5}},\ 3e^{-i\frac{3\pi}{5}}$.

subparts.text: Indicate clearly on an Argand diagram the points $Z_{0},\ Z_{1},\ Z_{2},\ Z_{3}$ and $Z_{4}$ which represent the roots found in (i). Deduce the perimeter of the polygon formed by the 5 points, giving your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: The 5 points lie on a circle of radius 3 centred at $O$, spaced $\frac{2\pi}{5}$ apart (a regular pentagon); perimeter $= 17.6$
subparts.solution:
All five roots have modulus 3 and their arguments differ by $\frac{2\pi}{5}$,
so they are the vertices of a regular pentagon inscribed in the circle $|z| = 3$.
Each side subtends an angle $\frac{2\pi}{5}$ at the centre, so its length is
$2(3)\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right) = 6\sin 36^{\circ} = 3.5267\ldots$
Perimeter $= 5 \times 3.5267\ldots = 17.63\ldots = 17.6$ (1 d.p.).

parts.text:
Two fixed complex numbers $a$ and $ia$ are represented by $A$ and $B$ respectively such that $0 < \arg(a) < \frac{\pi}{2}$. On a single Argand diagram, sketch the loci
(i) $|z - a| = |z - ia|$,
(ii) $|z - a| = |a|$. [3]
The 2 loci intersect at a point $P$ which represents the complex number $w$ such that $\operatorname{Im}(w) > 0$. Express $w$ in terms of $a$. [1]
parts.label: b
parts.answer: (i) the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, which passes through $O$; (ii) the circle centre $A$ (i.e. $a$) of radius $|a|$, passing through $O$; $w = a + ia$
parts.solution:
(i) $|z-a| = |z-ia|$ is the set of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$: the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
Since $|0-a| = |a| = |ia| = |0-ia|$, this bisector passes through the origin.
(ii) $|z-a| = |a|$ is the circle with centre $A$ and radius $|a|$; it also passes through the origin.
The two loci meet at $O$ and at one further point $P$.
Try $w = a + ia$: $|w - a| = |ia| = |a|$, so $P$ lies on the circle;
and $|w - ia| = |a|= |w-a|$, so $P$ lies on the bisector.
$O$ is the intersection with the smaller imaginary part, so the one with $\operatorname{Im}(w) > 0$ is $w = a + ia$.

parts.text: A gold coin manufacturer claims that the masses of gold coins he produced have mean $6$ g and variance $0.64$ g$^{2}$. If this claim is not rejected at $10\%$ level of significance based on the mean mass obtained from a random sample of 100 gold coins, between what values must the mean mass of the $100$ gold coins in the sample lie? State, giving a reason, whether any assumptions about the population are needed in order for the test to be valid.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: $5.8684 < \overline{x} < 6.1316$; no assumption is needed because $n = 100$ is large, so by the Central Limit Theorem $\overline{X}$ is approximately normal
parts.solution:
$H_{0}: \mu = 6$ against $H_{1}: \mu \neq 6$, a two-tailed test at the $10\%$ level.
The claim is not rejected when $|z| < 1.6449$, where $z = \frac{\overline{x}-6}{0.8/\sqrt{100}}$.
So $\left|\overline{x}-6\right| < 1.6449 \times 0.08 = 0.13159$,
giving $5.8684 < \overline{x} < 6.1316$ (4 d.p.).
No assumption about the population distribution is needed: $n = 100$ is large,
so by the Central Limit Theorem $\overline{X}$ is approximately normally distributed.

parts.text:
The manufacturer used a new coin making machine and claimed that the masses of gold coins produced by his new machine are not less than $6$ g. A random sample of 10 gold coins is taken and the mass, $x$ gram, of each gold coin is summarized as follows:
$$\sum(x - 4) = 14 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum(2x - 8)^{2} = 106.8$$
Find the unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance. [2]
Given that the masses of the gold coins follow a normal distribution, carry out a test at $5\%$ level of significance to determine whether the claim is justified. [4]
Explain, in the context of the question, the meaning of 'at $5\%$ level of significance'. [1]
parts.label: b
parts.answer: $\overline{x} = 5.4$, $s^{2} = 0.78889 \approx 0.789$; $p$-value $= 0.0307 < 0.05$, so reject $H_{0}$ — the claim is not justified. 'At $5\%$ level of significance' means there is a $0.05$ probability of wrongly concluding that the mean mass is less than 6 g when it is in fact 6 g.
parts.solution:
Unbiased estimates. With $n = 10$ and $\sum(x-4) = 14$:
$\overline{x} = 4 + \frac{14}{10} = 5.4$.
$\sum(2x-8)^{2} = 4\sum(x-4)^{2} = 106.8$, so $\sum(x-4)^{2} = 26.7$.
$s^{2} = \frac{1}{n-1}\left[\sum(x-4)^{2} - \frac{\left(\sum(x-4)\right)^{2}}{n}\right] = \frac{1}{9}\left[26.7 - \frac{14^{2}}{10}\right] = \frac{7.1}{9} = 0.78889 \approx 0.789.$
Test. $H_{0}: \mu = 6$ against $H_{1}: \mu < 6$, at the $5\%$ level.
Since the population is normal with unknown variance and $n = 10$ is small, use a $t$-test with $9$ degrees of freedom:
$$t = \frac{5.4-6}{\sqrt{0.78889/10}} = -2.1362.$$
$p$-value $= P(T < -2.1362) = 0.0307$.
Since $0.0307 < 0.05$, reject $H_{0}$: there is sufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level that the mean mass is less than 6 g,
so the manufacturer's claim is not justified.
Meaning. 'At $5\%$ level of significance' means there is a probability of $0.05$ of wrongly concluding that
the mean mass of the gold coins is less than 6 g when it is in fact 6 g.
SOURCE DEFECT: the paper prints $\sum(x-a) = 14$ with $a$ never defined. Reading it as $\sum(x-4) = 14$ reproduces BOTH printed key values ($\overline{x} = 5.4$ and $s^{2} = 0.78889$) exactly, so $a = 4$ and the corrected statement is stored.

stem: Given that $y=\frac{1}{2+\sin 2x}$, show that $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{2}{y}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}+4y^{2}\sin 2x$. [3]

parts.text: Hence find the Maclaurin series for $y$ up to and including the term in $x^{3}$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
First the result quoted in the stem. From $y\left(2+\sin 2x\right)=1$, differentiating gives $\frac{dy}{dx}\left(2+\sin 2x\right)+2y\cos 2x=0$, and since $\frac{1}{2+\sin 2x}=y$,
$\frac{dy}{dx}=-2y^{2}\cos 2x$
Differentiating again, $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-4y\frac{dy}{dx}\cos 2x+4y^{2}\sin 2x$, and $-4y\frac{dy}{dx}\cos 2x=-4y\cos 2x\cdot\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{y}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}$ because $-2y^{2}\cos 2x=\frac{dy}{dx}$. Hence $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{2}{y}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}+4y^{2}\sin 2x$ (shown).
At $x=0$: $y=\frac{1}{2}$, $\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)(1)=-\frac{1}{2}$, $\ \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{2}{\frac{1}{2}}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+0=1$.
Differentiating the given result, $\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}=\frac{4}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-\frac{2}{y^{2}}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3}+8y\frac{dy}{dx}\sin 2x+8y^{2}\cos 2x$.
At $x=0$: $\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}=\frac{4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)(1)}{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{2\left(-\frac{1}{8}\right)}{\frac{1}{4}}+0+8\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=-4+1+2=-1$.
$y=\frac{1}{2}+\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)x+\frac{1}{2!}(1)x^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}(-1)x^{3}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-\frac{1}{6}x^{3}$

parts.text: By considering the standard series for $\sin x$, verify that the series obtained in (i) is correct.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$\sin 2x=2x-\frac{(2x)^{3}}{3!}+\ldots=2x-\frac{4}{3}x^{3}+\ldots$
$y=\frac{1}{2+2x-\frac{4}{3}x^{3}+\ldots}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+x-\frac{2}{3}x^{3}+\ldots\right)^{-1}$
$=\frac{1}{2}\left[1-\left(x-\frac{2}{3}x^{3}\right)+\left(x-\frac{2}{3}x^{3}\right)^{2}-\left(x\right)^{3}+\ldots\right]$
$=\frac{1}{2}\left[1-x+\frac{2}{3}x^{3}+x^{2}-x^{3}+\ldots\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[1-x+x^{2}-\frac{1}{3}x^{3}+\ldots\right]$
$=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-\frac{1}{6}x^{3}+\ldots$, which is the series found in (i).

stem: A sequence $u_{1}$, $u_{2}$, $u_{3}$, $\ldots$ is defined by the recurrence relation $u_{n}=\frac{n}{n-1}u_{n-1}+\frac{1}{n-1}$, $n\geq 2$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $u_{1}=a$ where $a$ is a constant.

parts.text: Use the method of mathematical induction to show that $u_{n}=(a+1)n-1$ for all positive integers $n$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Let $P_{n}$ be the statement $u_{n}=(a+1)n-1$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$.
When $n=1$: $(a+1)(1)-1=a=u_{1}$, so $P_{1}$ is true.
Assume $P_{k}$ is true for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$, i.e. $u_{k}=(a+1)k-1$.
Then $u_{k+1}=\frac{k+1}{k}u_{k}+\frac{1}{k}=\frac{k+1}{k}\left[(a+1)k-1\right]+\frac{1}{k}$
$=(a+1)(k+1)-\frac{k+1}{k}+\frac{1}{k}=(a+1)(k+1)-\frac{k}{k}=(a+1)(k+1)-1$
So $P_{k}$ true $\Rightarrow P_{k+1}$ true. Since $P_{1}$ is true, by mathematical induction $P_{n}$ is true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ (shown).

parts.text: If $a=1$, show that $\sum_{n=2}^{N}\frac{1}{u_{n}u_{n-1}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{2N-1}\right)$. [2] Hence find $\sum_{n=2}^{N}\frac{1}{(2n+9)(2n+7)}$. [3]
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
With $a=1$, $u_{n}=2n-1$, so $u_{n}u_{n-1}=(2n-1)(2n-3)$ and
$\frac{1}{(2n-1)(2n-3)}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2n-3}-\frac{1}{2n-1}\right)$
$\sum_{n=2}^{N}\frac{1}{u_{n}u_{n-1}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=2}^{N}\left(\frac{1}{2n-3}-\frac{1}{2n-1}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{2N-1}\right)$ by telescoping (shown).
For the second sum, $2n+7=2m-3$ and $2n+9=2m-1$ when $m=n+5$, so the term is $\frac{1}{(2m-1)(2m-3)}$ and $n=2,\ldots,N$ corresponds to $m=7,\ldots,N+5$.
$\sum_{m=7}^{N+5}=\sum_{m=2}^{N+5}-\sum_{m=2}^{6}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{2N+9}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{11}\right)$
$=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{11}-\frac{1}{2N+9}\right)$

stem:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of a series, $S_{n}$, is given by
$$S_{n}=\frac{1}{a}\left[1-(a-1)^{n}\right],\ \text{where }a\text{ is a constant and }a\neq 1,\ n\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$$
Obtain an expression for the $n$th term of the series, $T_{n}$, and prove that $S_{n}$ is a geometric series. [3]
If the sequence $\left\{T_{n}\right\}$ is now grouped as follows:
$\left(T_{1}\right)$, $\left(T_{2},\ T_{3},\ T_{4}\right)$, $\left(T_{5},\ T_{6},\ T_{7},\ T_{8},\ T_{9}\right),\ \ldots$
where each subsequent bracket has 2 terms more than the previous bracket, find

parts.text: the total number of terms in the first $n$ brackets.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
First the stem demand. For $n\geq 2$,
$T_{n}=S_{n}-S_{n-1}=\frac{1}{a}\left[\left(a-1\right)^{n-1}-\left(a-1\right)^{n}\right]=\frac{1}{a}(a-1)^{n-1}\left[1-(a-1)\right]=\frac{1}{a}(a-1)^{n-1}(2-a)$
and $T_{1}=S_{1}=\frac{1}{a}\left[1-(a-1)\right]=\frac{2-a}{a}$, which is the same expression with $n=1$.
$\frac{T_{n}}{T_{n-1}}=\frac{\frac{1}{a}(a-1)^{n-1}(2-a)}{\frac{1}{a}(a-1)^{n-2}(2-a)}=a-1$, a constant, so the series is geometric with first term $\frac{2-a}{a}$ and common ratio $a-1$.
The brackets contain $1,3,5,\ldots$ terms, so the first $n$ brackets contain
$1+3+5+\cdots+(2n-1)=\frac{n}{2}\left[1+(2n-1)\right]=n^{2}$ terms.

parts.text: the middle term of the $11$th bracket in terms of $a$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The first $10$ brackets contain $10^{2}=100$ terms, and the first $11$ brackets contain $11^{2}=121$ terms.
So the $11$th bracket holds $T_{101}$ to $T_{121}$, which is $21$ terms, and its middle term is the $11$th of these, $T_{111}$.
$T_{111}=\frac{1}{a}(a-1)^{110}(2-a)$

parts.text: the range of values of $a$ for the sum to infinity of the series to exist. Hence, find the least value of $n$ for the sum of all the terms in the first $n$ brackets to be within $0.1\%$ of the sum to infinity of the series when $a=\frac{39}{20}$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
The sum to infinity exists when $|a-1|<1$, i.e. $-1<a-1<1$, so $0<a<2$ (and $a\neq 1$).
Then $S_{\infty}=\frac{1}{a}$, and the sum of all the terms in the first $n$ brackets is $S_{n^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}\left[1-(a-1)^{n^{2}}\right]$.
$\left|S_{\infty}-S_{n^{2}}\right|<0.001\,S_{\infty}$ gives $\frac{1}{a}\left|a-1\right|^{n^{2}}<0.001\cdot\frac{1}{a}$, i.e. $|a-1|^{n^{2}}<0.001$.
With $a=\frac{39}{20}$, $a-1=\frac{19}{20}=0.95$, so $0.95^{n^{2}}<0.001$.
$n^{2}\ln 0.95<\ln 0.001\Rightarrow n^{2}>\frac{\ln 0.001}{\ln 0.95}=134.67$
$n>11.605$, so the least value of $n$ is $12$.

subparts.text:
The complex numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfy the simultaneous equations
$$p^{*}+10i=qi+5$$
$$|p|^{2}-q-5+2i=0$$
Given that $\operatorname{Im}(p)<0$, find $p$ in the Cartesian form. [3] Hence find the value of $n$ for which $p^{2n}$ is purely imaginary. [2]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
From the second equation, $q=|p|^{2}-5+2i$. Substituting into the first,
$p^{*}+10i=i\left(|p|^{2}-5+2i\right)+5=|p|^{2}i-5i-2+5=3+\left(|p|^{2}-5\right)i$
Let $p=x+iy$, so $p^{*}=x-iy$ and $|p|^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$:
$x+(10-y)i=3+\left(x^{2}+y^{2}-5\right)i$
Comparing real parts: $x=3$.
Comparing imaginary parts: $10-y=9+y^{2}-5$, so $y^{2}+y-6=0$ and $y=-3$ or $y=2$.
Since $\operatorname{Im}(p)<0$, $y=-3$ and $p=3-3i$.
Then $|p|=3\sqrt{2}$ and $\arg p=-\frac{\pi}{4}$, so $\arg\left(p^{2n}\right)=2n\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=-\frac{n\pi}{2}$.
$p^{2n}$ is purely imaginary when $-\frac{n\pi}{2}=\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2}$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, i.e. $n=-(2k+1)$.
As $k$ ranges over $\mathbb{Z}$ this is exactly the set of odd integers, so $n=2k+1$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.

subparts.text: The complex number $w$ is such that $\arg\left(\frac{w}{p}-p^{*}\right)=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $w+w^{*}=-2$. Find $w$.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Let $w=x+iy$. From $w+w^{*}=-2$ we get $2x=-2$, so $x=-1$.
$\frac{w}{p}-p^{*}=\frac{w-pp^{*}}{p}=\frac{w-|p|^{2}}{p}=\frac{w-18}{p}$
$\arg\left(\frac{w-18}{p}\right)=\arg(w-18)-\arg p=\arg(w-18)+\frac{\pi}{4}=-\frac{\pi}{2}$
So $\arg(w-18)=-\frac{3\pi}{4}$, where $w-18=-19+iy$.
An argument of $-\frac{3\pi}{4}$ places the point in the third quadrant, so $y<0$ and
$-\left(\pi-\tan^{-1}\frac{|y|}{19}\right)=-\frac{3\pi}{4}\Rightarrow\tan^{-1}\frac{|y|}{19}=\frac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow|y|=19$
Hence $y=-19$ and $w=-1-19i$.
Check: $\frac{w}{p}=\frac{-1-19i}{3-3i}=\frac{(-1-19i)(3+3i)}{18}=\frac{54-60i}{18}=3-\frac{10}{3}i$, so $\frac{w}{p}-p^{*}=3-\frac{10}{3}i-(3+3i)=-\frac{19}{3}i$, whose argument is $-\frac{\pi}{2}$.

parts.text: Find the roots of the equation $\left(z-\sqrt{2}\right)^{6}=8$, giving your answer in the form $R\cos\theta\,e^{i\theta}$ where $R>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\leq\pi$. [3] Describe the curve on which all these roots lie. [1]
parts.label: b
parts.answer: $z=2\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\frac{k\pi}{6}\right)e^{\frac{k\pi}{6}i}$ for $k=0,\ \pm 1,\ \pm 2,\ 3$; the roots lie on the circle with centre $\left(\sqrt{2},0\right)$ and radius $\sqrt{2}$.
parts.solution:
$\left(z-\sqrt{2}\right)^{6}=8=8e^{i(2k\pi)}$, so $z-\sqrt{2}=8^{\frac{1}{6}}e^{\frac{k\pi}{3}i}=\sqrt{2}\,e^{\frac{k\pi}{3}i}$ for $k=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,3$.
$z=\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}e^{\frac{k\pi}{3}i}=\sqrt{2}e^{\frac{k\pi}{6}i}\left(e^{-\frac{k\pi}{6}i}+e^{\frac{k\pi}{6}i}\right)=2\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\frac{k\pi}{6}\right)e^{\frac{k\pi}{6}i}$
Since $\left|z-\sqrt{2}\right|=\sqrt{2}$ for every root, all the roots lie on the circle with centre $\left(\sqrt{2},0\right)$ and radius $\sqrt{2}$.

parts.text: The Yummy Confectionery manufactures candies from different fruits and randomly packs them in packets of $20$. It is known that $56\%$ of the candies are made from mangoes, $20\%$ from strawberries and the rest from lemons. A supermarket buys $60$ packets of candies from Yummy Confectionery. Find the probability that the average number of lemon candies in each packet is not less than $5$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
The proportion of lemon candies is $1-0.56-0.20=0.24$.
Let $L$ be the number of lemon candies in a packet, so $L\sim B(20,\ 0.24)$ with
$E(L)=20(0.24)=4.8$ and $\operatorname{Var}(L)=20(0.24)(0.76)=3.648$.
Since $n=60$ is large, by the Central Limit Theorem the sample mean $\bar{L}$ of the $60$ packets is approximately normal:
$\bar{L}\sim N\left(4.8,\ \frac{3.648}{60}\right)=N(4.8,\ 0.0608)$ approximately.
$P\left(\bar{L}\geq 5\right)=P\left(Z\geq\frac{5-4.8}{\sqrt{0.0608}}\right)=P(Z\geq 0.8111)=0.20865$
$\approx 0.209$

parts.text: The confectionery wishes to test the popularity of a new flavour among people of all ages by surveying $300$ people. Comment on the suitability of the sample if the survey is administered to $300$ randomly selected students from various secondary schools. [1] Give a reason why it would be difficult to use a stratified sample and suggest a suitable sampling method. [2]
parts.label: ii
parts.answer: The sample is unsuitable: secondary-school students are not representative of people of all ages, so the sample is biased. A stratified sample is difficult because there is no sampling frame giving the sizes of the age groups in the population from which to draw proportionally. Quota sampling is a suitable alternative.
parts.solution:
The company wants the views of people of all ages, but every member of the proposed sample is a secondary-school student, roughly $13$ to $17$ years old.
The sample is therefore not representative of the target population and the results would be biased, even though the students are chosen at random.
For a stratified sample the population must first be divided into strata (here, age groups) and the size of each stratum must be known so that the sample can be shared out in proportion. No such sampling frame or list of the whole population by age is available to the company, so a stratified sample is impractical.
Quota sampling is suitable: the interviewer simply keeps surveying until the required number in each age group has been obtained, which needs no sampling frame.

stem: During an $8$-hour workday, the telephone switchboard at Global Enterprise receives an average of $1$ prank call per hour.

parts.text: State a condition under which a Poisson distribution would be a suitable probability model for the number of prank calls received. $[1]$ Assume that the number of prank calls received follows a Poisson distribution. Find the probability that there will be at most $5$ prank calls in a workday. $[2]$
parts.label: a
parts.answer: Condition: prank calls occur randomly and independently, at a constant average rate throughout the workday (equivalently, the numbers received in non-overlapping intervals are independent). Probability $= 0.191$ (3 s.f.)
parts.solution:
**Condition.** Either of the following is acceptable:

- the average number of prank calls received is constant throughout the workday and the calls occur randomly and independently of one another; or
- the numbers of prank calls received in non-overlapping time intervals are independent.

**Probability.** Over an $8$-hour workday the mean number of calls is $8 \times 1 = 8$, so $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(8)$.

$\mathrm{P}(X \leq 5) = e^{-8}\left( 1 + 8 + \dfrac{8^{2}}{2!} + \dfrac{8^{3}}{3!} + \dfrac{8^{4}}{4!} + \dfrac{8^{5}}{5!} \right) = 0.191236 = 0.191$ (3 s.f.)

(The $1$-mark condition is stored with this part because a question that carries parts keeps all its solutions on the parts; the printed mark split is kept inline.)

parts.text: The probability that there will be at least two workdays in $n$ workdays with at most $5$ prank calls in a workday is more than $0.755$. Find the least value of $n$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let $Y$ be the number of workdays out of $n$ with at most $5$ prank calls. Then $Y \sim \mathrm{B}(n,\; 0.191236)$.

$\mathrm{P}(Y \geq 2) > 0.755 \Rightarrow 1 - \mathrm{P}(Y = 0) - \mathrm{P}(Y = 1) > 0.755$

Trying values of $n$:

$n = 13$: $\mathrm{P}(Y \geq 2) = 0.74196$ — not enough.

$n = 14$: $\mathrm{P}(Y \geq 2) = 0.77919 > 0.755$ ✓

Since $\mathrm{P}(Y \geq 2)$ increases with $n$, the least value is $n = 14$.

parts.text: Find the probability that there will be an average of more than $1.2$ prank calls in an hour over ten $8$-hour workdays.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Ten workdays is $10 \times 8 = 80$ hours. Let $T$ be the total number of prank calls in that time; by the additive property of the Poisson distribution,

$T \sim \mathrm{Po}(80)$

An average of more than $1.2$ calls per hour over $80$ hours means

$\dfrac{T}{80} > 1.2 \Rightarrow T > 96 \Rightarrow T \geq 97$

$\mathrm{P}(T \geq 97) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(T \leq 96) = 0.0355915 = 0.0356$ (3 s.f.)

(Source note: the key prints "$0.035591 \approx 0.356$" — the rounded figure has a misplaced decimal point; the correct $3$ s.f. value is $0.0356$.)

parts.text: Global Enterprise will make a police report if there are at least $4$ consecutive workdays in a week during which more than $5$ prank calls are received in a day. Assuming the company operates from Monday to Friday only, show that the probability that a police report is made in a particular week is $0.510$, correct to $3$ significant figures.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
For a single workday, $\mathrm{P}(X > 5) = 1 - 0.191236 = 0.808764$; call this $q$.

With five workdays (Mon–Fri), "at least $4$ consecutive high days" happens in exactly these ways:

- Mon–Thu all high: probability $q^{4}$
- Tue–Fri all high: probability $q^{4}$
- all five high: probability $q^{5}$ — counted in **both** of the above, so subtract once.

$\mathrm{P}(\text{report}) = 2q^{4} - q^{5} = 2(0.808764)^{4} - (0.808764)^{5}$

$= 2(0.427857) - 0.346050 = 0.509665 = 0.510$ (3 s.f.) (shown)
